leads.caseName: Zavala Family Inc. v. Super. Ct.
leads.text:
Filed 11/24/26 
CERTIFIED FOR PUBLICATION 
 
IN THE COURT OF APPEAL OF THE STATE OF CALIFORNIA 
 
SECOND APPELLATE DISTRICT 
 
DIVISION EIGHT 
 
ZAVALA FAMILY INC.  et al.,  
 Petitioners; 
 v. 
THE SUPERIOR COURT OF 
LOS ANGELES COUNTY,  
 Respondent; 
LOS ANGELES COUNTY 
METROPOLITAN 
TRANSPORTATION 
AUTHORITY,  
 Real Party in Interest. 
B352255 
Los Angeles County 
Super. Ct. No. 25VECV05690 
 
PETITION for a writ of mandate from an order of the 
Superior Court of Los Angeles County.  Shirley K. Watkins, 
Judge.  Petition denied. 
California Eminent Domain Law Group, Glenn L. Block; 
Pierson Ferdinand and Paul J. Beard II, for Petitioners. 
No appearance for Respondent. 
FBT Gibbons, Keith E. McCullough, S. Christopher Yoo 
and Andrew M. Jones for Real Party in Interest. 
2 
 _________________________ 
We encounter the intersection of eminent domain and 
unlawful detainer.  Real party Los Angeles Metropolitan 
Transportation Authority (Metro) acquired, under threat of 
condemnation, real property that petitioners Zavala Family Inc. 
and Jose Zavala had leased to run a scrap metal recycling 
business.  When petitioners remained on the premises after 
Metro’s acquisition, Metro sought possession of the premises 
through an unlawful detainer action.  The parties dispute 
whether the unlawful detainer action can proceed, or whether 
Metro must instead seek possession through procedures set forth 
in the Eminent Domain Law (Code Civ. Proc., § 1230.010 et seq.).  
(Undesignated statutory references are to the Code of Civil 
Procedure.)  The trial court, rejecting the arguments in 
petitioners’ demurrer, concluded Metro’s unlawful detainer action 
could proceed.  Petitioners seek a writ of mandate directing the 
trial court to sustain their demurrer.  We deny their petition.  We 
do not conclude that an unlawful detainer action will always be 
an appropriate method for determining a tenant’s possessory 
interest in real property acquired under threat of condemnation; 
rather, we reject petitioners’ limited arguments against the use of 
unlawful detainer in this case.  
I. 
We take the facts from the unlawful detainer complaint 
and consider, for context, undisputed facts admitted in the writ 
petition pleadings or reflected in documents attached to Metro’s 
March 25, 2026 unopposed motion for judicial notice, which we 
grant.  We deny two other requests for judicial notice:  one 
petitioners filed February 9, 2026, seeking notice of filings in 
other pending eminent domain actions, and one Metro filed 
3 
February 17, 2026, seeking notice of petitioners’ answer to the 
complaint.  The documents attached to these two earlier requests 
do not bear upon our resolution of the issues presented in this 
writ proceeding.  (OneTaste Inc. v. Netflix, Inc. (2025) 
116 Cal.App.5th 174, 194 [denial of judicial notice proper for 
irrelevant and unnecessary documents].)   
Since at least April 2017, petitioners have operated a scrap 
metal recycling business on a parcel of real property located in 
Van Nuys, California.  Petitioners leased these premises from 
Franz J. Neuwirth and Gretchen V. Newell, Trustees of The Etzel 
Trust UTA January 7, 2021 (collectively, “Etzel Trust”).  The 
written lease is not in the record before us.  
 In September 2023, Metro sent petitioners written notice of 
its intent to acquire the premises to construct the East San 
Fernando Valley Light Rail Transit Project.  The notice informed 
petitioners of their potential eligibility for relocation benefits 
under the Uniform Relocation Assistance and Real Property 
Acquisition Policies Act of 1970 (42 U.S.C. § 4601 et seq.).  The 
notice stated, in bolded text, that petitioners “will not be required 
to move without at least 90 days advance written notice of the 
day by which [they] must vacate.” 
 In February 2024, Metro sent petitioners written notice 
that it had made an offer to purchase the premises in December 
2023 and again advised petitioners of their potential eligibility 
for relocation benefits.  The notice advised, in bolded text, “you 
are not requested or required to move as a result of this notice” 
and if Metro “acquires the property, you will be given at least 90 
days written notice before you will be required to move.” 
 Four months later, in June 2024, the Etzel Trust 
contracted to sell the real property to Metro.  The Etzel Trust 
4 
conveyed the property to Metro through a grant deed recorded on 
January 23, 2025. 
 About a month later, on February 21, 2025, Metro sent 
petitioners a 30-day notice to vacate the premises.  Subsequently, 
it sent a second 30-day notice on March 14, 2025, and a third 30-
day notice on May 14, 2025.  Petitioners continued to occupy the 
premises. 
 Approximately five months after the third notice, on 
October 6, 2025, Metro filed an unlawful detainer action seeking 
immediate possession of the premises.  The complaint alleged 
Metro “acquired the Premises for public use” and, consequently, 
by operation of section 1265.110, “any leasehold interest in the 
Premises held by Defendants was . . . terminated effective on 
[Metro’s] acquisition of the Premises” in January 2025.  The 
complaint alleged that because petitioners have not entered into 
a new lease or other agreement with Metro permitting their 
continued occupation of the premises, petitioners “became a 
holdover tenant without any leasehold interest” subject to 
eviction under section 1161, subdivision (1). 
 Three days later, Metro filed a complaint in eminent 
domain to “acquire improvements . . . located on” the premises 
petitioners occupied to further “the East San Fernando Valley 
Light Rail Transit Project.”  
 Petitioners demurred to the unlawful detainer complaint.  
Petitioners asserted the trial court lacked jurisdiction (see 
§ 430.10, subd. (a)) over the premises at issue in the unlawful 
detainer case because section 1230.050 operated to confer 
exclusive jurisdiction over the premises to the eminent domain 
court.  Petitioners also asserted the complaint failed to state facts 
sufficient to constitute a cause of action (§ 430.10, subd. (e)) 
5 
because, in their view, section 1265.110, which terminates a lease 
upon acquisition of property for public use, only terminates a 
tenant’s liability for rent, and does not affect a tenant’s 
possessory rights.  In petitioners’ view, Metro needed to seek 
possession of the premises in accord with the Eminent Domain 
Law and its procedural safeguards, most notably section 
1255.410, which concerns prejudgment possession.  Finally, 
petitioners asserted the complaint must be dismissed because the 
eminent domain and unlawful detainer cases concerned the same 
parties and the same causes of action.  (§ 430.10, subd. (c).)   
 The trial court overruled the demurrer.  
 Petitioners filed a petition for writ of mandate in this court 
requesting that we vacate the trial court’s order and instruct that 
court to instead sustain the demurrer without leave to amend.  
Metro filed a preliminary opposition.  Petitioners filed a 
preliminary reply.  
We temporarily stayed the unlawful detainer action and 
directed the trial court to show cause why the petitioners’ 
requested relief should not be granted.  Thereafter, Metro filed a 
return, and petitioners filed a reply. 
II. 
 “ ‘The standard of review for an order overruling a 
demurrer is de novo.  The reviewing court accepts as true all facts 
properly pleaded in the complaint in order to determine whether 
the demurrer should be overruled.  [Citation.]’  [Citation.]  We 
must also consider matters that are properly the subject of 
judicial notice.”  (Big Valley Band of Pomo Indians v. Superior 
Court (2005) 133 Cal.App.4th 1185, 1190.)  “We do not accept as 
true the pleader’s deductions, contentions, or conclusions of law, 
as this court must decide questions of law independently.”  (Doe 
6 
3, Family Services Organization v. Superior Court (2025) 
110 Cal.App.5th 571, 582 (Doe 3).)   
 “To the extent the trial court’s ruling on a demurrer 
presents a question of statutory interpretation, we will interpret 
the statute de novo as well.  [Citation.]  Our task in interpreting 
a statute is to determine the Legislature’s intent in order to 
effectuate the law’s purpose, first by looking at the plain and 
commonsense meaning of the statutory language.  [Citations.]  
We examine the language in the context of the statutory scheme 
as a whole to determine the law’s scope and purpose, and to 
harmonize the various parts of the enactment.  [Citation.]  ‘If the 
language of the statute is ambiguous, we “can look to legislative 
history [citation] and to rules or maxims of construction” to 
resolve the ambiguity.  [Citation.]’ ”  (Doe 3, supra, 
110 Cal.App.5th at p. 582.)   
 In this proceeding, petitioners renew several of their 
demurrer arguments for why Metro cannot proceed by unlawful 
detainer.  That is, petitioners assert section 1230.050 requires a 
condemning entity to secure possession of any property taken for 
public use through the Eminent Domain Law, section 1265.110 
cannot authorize an unlawful detainer action because it does not 
terminate a lease, and Metro must comply with section 
1255.410’s procedures to obtain possession.  To the extent 
petitioners’ demurrer raised other arguments against an 
unlawful detainer proceeding, including that dismissal is 
required under section 430.10, subdivision (c), because of another 
action pending, we do not address them.  (See Golden Door 
Properties, LLC v. County of San Diego (2020) 50 Cal.App.5th 
467, 554–555 [“ ‘Even when our review . . . “is de novo, it is 
limited to issues which have been adequately raised and 
7 
supported in [the appellant’s opening] brief” ’ ”and “ ‘ “[i]ssues not 
raised in an appellant’s brief are deemed” ’ ” forfeited]; see also 
In re Reno (2012) 55 Cal.4th 428, 458, fn. 15 [writ review is 
typically limited to only those issues properly raised].)  We 
emphasize, then, the limited nature of the petition, its challenge 
to the unlawful detainer process, and its arguments for relief.  
Just by way of example, petitioners have not advanced, and we 
will not address, arguments against the unlawful detainer 
process based on Metro’s simultaneous seeking of improvements 
in eminent domain or those improvements’ existence, nature, and 
relationship to the acquired premises.  (Cf. Chhour v. Community 
Redevelopment Agency (1996) 46 Cal.App.4th 273, 282–283.) 
A. 
 Petitioners assert that under section 1230.050 and, in 
particular, under the Law Revision Commission’s comment to 
that section, an eminent domain court has exclusive jurisdiction 
to determine possession of property acquired for public use and 
that Metro’s unlawful detainer action is, for that reason, 
impermissible.  Section 1230.050 grants the court presiding over 
an eminent domain action “the power” to “[d]etermine the right to 
possession of the property, as between the plaintiff and the 
defendant, in accordance with” the Eminent Domain Law and to 
“[e]nforce any of its orders for possession by appropriate process.”  
(§ 1230.050, subds. (a)–(b); see § 1230.010.)  The Law Revision 
Commission’s comment explains that, “[i]n general,” section 
1230.050 “codifies judicial decisions which hold that, after an 
eminent domain proceeding is begun, the court in which that 
proceeding is pending has the exclusive power to determine the 
respective rights of the plaintiff and of the defendant to 
possession and to enforce its determinations.”  (Cal. Law Revision 
8 
Com. com., Deering’s Ann. Code Civ. Proc., § 1230.050 (1975) 
p. 1069.)  
 In support of this proposition, the Law Revision 
Commission’s comment cites three cases, one of which, San 
Bernardino Valley Municipal Water Dist. v. Gage Canal Co. 
(1964) 226 Cal.App.2d 206 (San Bernardino), addresses the 
extent of an eminent domain court’s “exclusive power” (Cal. Law

NOT FOR PUBLICATION IN WEST'S HAWAI#I REPORTS AND PACIFIC REPORTER 
Electronically Filed 
Intermediate Court of Appeals 
CAAP-24-0000649 
24-NOV-2026 
08:00 AM 
Dkt. 97 SO 
NO. CAAP-24-0000649 
IN THE INTERMEDIATE COURT OF APPEALS 
OF THE STATE OF 
HAWAI#I 
ONE WAILEA DEVELOPMENT LLC, Appellant-Appellant, v.
MAUI PLANNING COMMISSION, Appellee-Appellee
and WAILEA SF-S PARTNERS LP, Appellee/Intervenor-Appellee 
APPEAL FROM THE CIRCUIT COURT OF THE SECOND CIRCUIT 
(CASE NO. 2CCV-23-0000154) 
SUMMARY DISPOSITION ORDER 
(By: Leonard, Presiding Judge, Hiraoka and Guidry, JJ.) 
The Maui County 
Planning Commission granted a Special 
Management Area Use 
Permit to One Wailea Development LLC in 
June 1999. The Planning Commission decided to "close and/or 
terminate" the Permit on February 14, 2023. LLC appealed the 
Planning Commission's Findings of Fact, Conclusions of Law, 
Decision and Order Closing Subject SMA Permit SM1 1999/0010 to 
the Circuit Court of the Second Circuit. The circuit court 
affirmed the Decision and Order, granted the Planning 
Commission's motion for sanctions, and entered a Final Judgment.
1 
LLC filed this secondary appeal. We affirm. 
In May 1999, Michael J. Szymanski  contracted to buy 
21.3 acres of real Property on Maui from Wailea Resort Company. 
Szymanski then formed LLC; he is its sole member and manager. 
Szymanski planned to use LLC to develop the Property into twenty 
single-family home lots. 
1 The Honorable Kirstin M. Hamman presided.  
 
NOT FOR PUBLICATION IN WEST'S HAWAI#I REPORTS AND PACIFIC REPORTER 
The Property is located in a Coastal Zone Management 
Special Management Area (SMA). Development in an SMA requires a 
permit. Hawaii Revised Statutes (HRS) § 205A-28 (2017). LLC 
applied to the Maui County Planning Department for an SMA use 
permit in June 1999. The Planning Commission's SMA Rules 
required the applicant to provide "documentation of ownership or 
authorization by the owners of the parcel on which the proposed 
action is to occur[.]" SMA Rules § 12-202-12(c)(2)(A).
2  LLC's 
application included a letter from Wailea Resort Co. authorizing 
LLC to apply for the SMA use permit. 
By letter dated November 24, 1999, the Planning 
Department informed LLC that the Planning Commission had approved 
its permit application, subject to conditions. LLC had to start 
construction by November 30, 2001, and construction had to be 
completed within five years. 
Beginning in October 2001 LLC asked for, and received, 
several extensions of the deadline to begin construction because 
Szymanski was "working with the seller to complete the sale" of 
the Property. 
The Szymanski-Wailea Resort Co. transaction did not go 
well. In July 2002, Title Guaranty Escrow Services filed an
Interpleader Action for funds it held in escrow. Title Guar. 
Escrow Servs., Inc. v. Wailea Resort Co., 146 Hawai#i 34, 38, 456 
P.3d 107, 111 (2019) (Title Guaranty). Szymanski and Wailea 
2 SMA Rules § 12-202-12 (eff. Sept. 28, 1997) provided: 
(c) Assessment applications shall be filed in
accordance with the following: 
. . . . 
(2) Any applicant seeking an assessment shall submit
an application form, provided by the department,
to the central coordinating agency. The 
application shall require the following
information and documentation: 
(A) Identification of the applicant along with
documentation of ownership or
authorization by the owners of the parcel
on which the proposed action is to
occur[.] 
2 
NOT FOR PUBLICATION IN WEST'S HAWAI#I REPORTS AND PACIFIC REPORTER 
Resort Co. filed cross-claims. Id. Each claimed the other had 
breached their Land Sales Contract. 
In September 2002 LLC asked for a 90-day extension of 
the deadline to complete construction because it was in "the 
final stages of closing the transaction and are awaiting the 
partial mortgage release from the seller's Japanese lender." The 
Planning Department stated it would hold LLC's request "in 
abeyance until December 31, 2002, however, 
this will be the last deferral to be granted. After this date 
the request will be forwarded to the Maui Planning Commission for 
appropriate action." 
In December 2002 LLC asked for another extension of the 
deadline to complete construction. In January 2003 the Planning 
Department asked Wailea Resort Co. whether it continued to 
authorize LLC to proceed to develop the Property. In February 
2003 LLC's attorney told the Planning Department about the 
Interpleader Action and opined that LLC was likely to "obtain a 
decree of specific performance requiring [Wailea Resort Co.] to 
comply with the Contract and convey the [P]roperty to Szymanski." 
It appears that the Planning Department took no further action 
pending resolution of the Interpleader Action. 
In 2004 the trial court presiding over the Interpleader 
Action granted summary judgment on Szymanski's and Wailea 
Resort Co.'s cross-claims. The court ruled that Szymanski 
breached the Land Sales Contract and was not entitled to specific 
performance by Wailea Resort Co. The 2004 Summary Judgment was 
certified as final under Hawai#i Rules of Civil Procedure (HRCP) 
Rule 54(b). Szymanski appealed. 
We affirmed. Title Guar. 
Escrow Servs., Inc. v. Szymanski, No. 27254, 2009 WL 1112604 
(Haw. App. Apr. 27, 2009) (SDO), cert. rejected
, 2009 WL 2974724 
(Haw. Sept. 17, 2009). The only issue remaining was who should 
receive the interpleaded funds. 
Szymanski nevertheless continued to challenge the 2004 
Summary Judgment. He moved to vacate the 2004 Summary Judgment, 
arguing the judge who entered it should have recused. See Title 
Guaranty
, 146 Hawai#i at 39, 456 P.3d at 112. The motion was 
denied. Id.
 at 40, 456 P.3d at 113. Szymanski moved for 
3 
NOT FOR PUBLICATION IN WEST'S HAWAI#I REPORTS AND PACIFIC REPORTER 
reconsideration. Id. Reconsideration was denied. Id.
Szymanski appealed. We affirmed. Title Guar. Escrow Servs., 
Inc. v. Wailea Resort Co., No. CAAP–12–0000711, 2016 WL 4555771 
(Haw. App. Aug. 31, 2016) (mem. op.), cert. rejected, 2017 WL 
127710 (Haw. Jan. 12, 2017), cert. rejected, 2018 WL 5817276 
(Haw. Nov. 7, 2018), cert. denied. sub nom., Szymanski v. Wailea 
Resort Co., 583 U.S. 827, 138 S. Ct. 164, 199 L. Ed. 2d 39 
(2017). 
Undaunted, "Szymanski filed yet another motion to 
vacate" the 2004 Summary Judgment based on the trial judge's 
failure to recuse. Title Guaranty, 146 Hawai#i at 41, 456 P.3d 
at 114. 
The motion was denied. Id. at 42, 456 P.3d at 115. 
Szymanski appealed. 
We affirmed. Title Guar. Escrow Servs., 
Inc. v. Wailea Resort Co., Nos. CAAP-14-0001138 and 
CAAP-16-0000034, 2018 WL 3198379 (Haw. App. June 29, 2018) (SDO), 
aff'd in part, vacated in part, 146 Hawai#i 34, 456 P.3d 107 
(2019). 
On certiorari, the supreme court affirmed the denial of 
the motion to vacate the 2004 Summary Judgment. Title Guaranty, 
146 Hawai#i at 46, 456 P.3d at 119 (holding that "the ICA did not 
err in applying the law of the case doctrine with respect to 
Szymanski's 2014 Renewed Motion to Vacate Judge Loo's 2004 
Summary Judgment Orders that again asserted Judge Loo should have 
been disqualified"). The 2019 Title Guaranty decision 
conclusively affirmed that Szymanski breached the Land Sales 
Contract and was not entitled to specific performance by Wailea 
Resort Co. The supreme court also held that we erred by 
affirming the circuit court's disbursal of the escrowed funds to 
Wailea Resort Co., and remanded to the circuit court for 
disposition of the funds. Id. at 48-49, 456 P.3d at 121-22. 
On October 6, 2020, the Planning Department notified 
LLC it had determined that LLC had neither an ownership interest 
in, nor authorization from Wailea Resort Co. to develop, the 
Property. The Planning Department closed LLC's Permit. 
LLC requested a contested case hearing. A hearing 
officer was appointed. The hearing officer proposed findings of 
fact and conclusions of law, and recommended a decision. The 
4
 
NOT FOR PUBLICATION IN WEST'S HAWAI#I REPORTS AND PACIFIC REPORTER 
Planning Commission adopted the hearing officer's report and 
recommendation, and entered the Decision and Order on 
February 14, 2023. LLC requested reconsideration. The Planning 
Commission denied reconsideration. 
LLC appealed to the circuit court. The circuit court 
affirmed the Decision and Order. The court also granted the 
Planning Commission's motion for HRCP Rule 11 sanctions against 
LLC. The Final Judgment was entered on June 6, 2024. LLC moved 
for reconsideration. Reconsideration was denied. This secondary 
appeal followed. 
(1) LLC contends the circuit court "made numerous 
procedural errors, and numerous factual and legal errors." But 
in this secondary appeal, we apply the standards in HRS 
§ 91-14(g) (2012 & Supp. 2019) to the Planning Commission's 
Decision and Order, not to the circuit court's order affirming 
it. Sierra Club v. D.R. Horton-Schuler Homes, LLC, 136 Hawai#i 
505, 515–16, 364 P.3d 213, 223–24 (2015). 
LLC contends the Decision and Order was arbitrary and 
capricious and should be vacated under HRS § 91-14(g)(6). LLC 
challenges the Planning Commission's findings of fact (FOF) 
nos. 55 and 56. The Planning Commission's other findings of 
fact, which are unchallenged, are binding on appeal. Okada 
Trucking Co. v. Bd. of Water Supply, 97 Hawai#i 450, 459, 40 P.3d 
73, 82 (2002). 
The Decision and Order stated: 
55. The Supreme Court remanded the matter to the Circuit
Court only as to the deposit issue: "[W]e vacate the ICA's
judgment on appeal only as to the disbursal of escrow funds
to [WRC]. This case is remanded to the circuit court for 
further proceedings consistent with this opinion."
(December 24, 2019 Hawaii Supreme Court decision[.]) 
56. As a result of these court appeals regarding the
status of the Land Sales Contract, it has now been
judicially determined that: 
a. Szymanski was the party in breach of obligations
under the Land Sales Contract; 
b. Szymanski is not entitled to an order directing
that the Land Sales Contract should be specifically
performed such that Szymanski would become the party
entitled to be the owner and successful buyer of the
Subject Property; 
5 
 
NOT FOR PUBLICATION IN WEST'S HAWAI#I REPORTS AND PACIFIC REPORTER 
c. The Land Sales Contract has been terminated, and 
d. The only remaining issue to be determined is a
question of who is entitled to receive the
interpleaded escrow funds of $50,000 and associated
interest. (December 24, 2019 Hawaii Supreme Court
decision[.]) 
The label finding of fact or conclusion of law does not 
determine the standard of review. Pave v. Prod. Processing, 
Inc., 152 Hawai#i 164, 171, 524 P.3d 355, 362 (App. 2022). 
Whether a determination is a finding of fact, a conclusion of 
law, or a mixed finding and conclusion is a question of law 
freely reviewable on appeal. Id. FOF nos. 55 and 56 were 
actually conclusions of law construing the 2019 Title Guaranty 
decision. 
We review an agency's conclusions of law de novo under 
the right/wrong standard. Sierra Club, 136 Hawai#i at 516, 364 
P.3d at 224. The supreme court's 2019 
Title Guaranty decision 
conclusively affirmed that Szymanski breached the contract to buy 
the Property and was not entitled to specific performance by 
Wailea Resort Co. 
FOF nos. 55 and 56 were right. 
The Planning Commission then concluded: 
13. Szymanski and [LLC] do not have any ownership
interest in the Subject Property nor any contractual right
to purchase or acquire an interest in the Subject Property
and have no authorization from the owner of the Subject
Property to pursue a SMA permit. Consequently, [LLC] and
Szymanski do not qualify for and are not entitled to be a
holder of an SMA permit for the Subject Property. 
14. Accordingly, it is appropriate for the
Department to close and/or terminate the subject SMA permit.

must provide "documents of ownership or authorization by the

leads.text:
FOR PUBLICATION 
 
UNITED STATES COURT OF APPEALS 
FOR THE NINTH CIRCUIT 
 
LOS MOLINOS MUTUAL WATER 
COMPANY; STANFORD VINA 
RANCH IRRIGATION COMPANY; 
PEYTON PACIFIC PROPERTIES, 
LLC, 
 
                     Plaintiffs - Appellants, 
 
   v. 
 
ERIK EKDAHL; EILEEN SOBECK; 
E. JOAQUIN ESQUIVEL, Board 
Chair; DORENE D’ADAMO; SEAN 
MAGUIRE; LAUREL FIRESTONE; 
NICHOLE MORGAN, 
 
                     Defendants - Appellees. 
 No. 25-2302 
D.C. No. 
2:21-cv-01961-
DAD-DMC 
 
 
OPINION 
 
Appeal from the United States District Court  
for the Eastern District of California 
Dale A. Drozd, District Judge, Presiding 
 
Argued and Submitted August 11, 2026 
Reno, Nevada 
 
Filed November 24, 2026 
 
2 LOS MOLINOS MUTUAL WATER CO. V. EKDAHL 
Before: John B. Owens, Danielle J. Forrest, and Lawrence 
VanDyke, Circuit Judges. 
 
Opinion by Judge VanDyke 
 
 
SUMMARY* 
 
Procedural Due Process 
 
The panel reversed the district court’s order dismissing 
the due process claims of Stanford Vina Ranch Irrigation 
Co., Los Molinos Mutual Water Co., and Peyton Pacific, 
LLC (collectively, “Plaintiffs”), in their action challenging 
2021 and 2022 emergency regulations and water curtailment 
orders promulgated by the California State Water Resources 
Control Board (“SWRCB”), and remanded. 
Plaintiffs are companies that hold the majority of riparian 
water rights in California’s Deer Creek and Mill Creek.   In 
2021 and 2022, in response to drought conditions, the 
SWRCB adopted emergency regulations and curtailment 
orders that ordered the twenty- two water rights holders on 
those creeks to reduce or stop diverting water. 
Plaintiffs allege that in both 2021 and 2022, they 
requested and were denied evidentiary hearings and the 
opportunity to cross -examine the SWRCB and California 
Department of Fish and Wildlife employees who testified in 
favor of the emergency orders.   Instead, Plaintiffs were 
 
* This summary constitutes no part of the opinion of the court.  It has 
been prepared by court staff for the convenience of the reader. 
 LOS MOLINOS MUTUAL WATER CO. V. EKDAHL 3 
allowed only five minutes during the public comment period 
at the 2021 meeting.  Plaintiffs sued in federal district court, 
raising, among others, procedural due process claims under 
the Fourteenth Amendment and takings claims under the 
Fifth Amendment, and seeking injuncti ve and declaratory 
relief. 
Addressing jurisdiction, the panel held that Plaintiffs’ 
claims were not moot.   Although the 2021 and 2022 
emergency regulations and curtailment orders are no longer 
in effect, the capable of repetition yet evading review 
exception applies here because: (1) the one-year duration of 
the emergency regulations and the eight -month duration of 
the curtailment orders are plainly too short to allow full 
litigation before the regulations and orders cease; and 
(2) Plaintiffs’ allegations are sufficient to show some 
indication that the challenged conduct will be repeated 
where between 2014 and 2022 Defendants enacted similar 
emergency regulations and curtailment orders four separate 
times and drought conditions likely will reoccur. 
Turning to Plaintiffs’ procedural due process claim, the 
panel concluded that Plaintiffs plausibly alleged a protected 
property interest in their adjudicated water rights to divert 
water from Deer and Mill Creeks. 
The panel next concluded that the district court erred by 
characterizing Defendants’ emergency regulations and 
curtailment orders as legislative, rather than 
adjudicatory.  Defendants’ actions were adjudicatory 
because they severely altered the permissible uses of 
Plaintiffs’ individual water rights, and the twenty-two water 
rights holders here are not so numerous in an absolute sense 
that it would be “impracticable” to allow them more than 
five minu tes to meaningfully describe how the proposed 
4 LOS MOLINOS MUTUAL WATER CO. V. EKDAHL 
governmental action will uniquely impact them.  Because 
the emergency regulations and curtailment orders were 
adjudicatory, due process required a meaningful pre -
deprivation hearing —which Plaintiffs did not 
receive.  Accordingly, the panel held that Plaintiffs 
adequately pled procedural due process claims, and the 
district court erred in dismissing those claims. 
The panel also reversed the district court’s dismissal of 
Plaintiffs’ request for declaratory relief with respect to their 
procedural due process claims.   
The panel affirmed the district court’s dismissal of 
Plaintiffs’ takings claims in a concurrently filed 
memorandum disposition. 
 
 
COUNSEL 
Jackson A. Minasian (argued) and Paul R. Minasian, 
Minasian Law LLP, Oroville, California, for Plaintiff -
Appellants. 
Margaret V. Tides (argued), Scott D. Cavanuagh, and Colin 
D. Smithey, Deputy Attorneys General; Sierra S. Arballo, 
Supervising Deputy Attorney General; Myung J. Park, 
Acting Senior Assistant Attorney General; Rob Bonta, 
California Attorney General; Office of the California 
Attorney General, Sacramento, California; for Defendants -
Appellees. 
 
 LOS MOLINOS MUTUAL WATER CO. V. EKDAHL 5 
OPINION 
VANDYKE, Circuit Judge: 
 
The plaintiffs in this case appeal from the district court’s 
dismissal of their procedural due process and takings claims.  
We reverse the dismissal of the due process claims  and 
remand.1 
I. Background 
Stanford Vina Ranch Irrigation Co., Los Molinos Mutual 
Water Co., and Peyton Pacific, LLC (collectively, 
“Plaintiffs”) are companies that hold the lion’s share of 
riparian water rights in California’s Deer Creek and Mill 
Creek, each of which  runs for about sixty miles.  Stanford 
Vina has the right to use “approximately 66% of the flow of 
Deer Creek,” which it uses for agricultural purposes over a 
5,700-acre area.  Los Molinos Mutual Water Co. holds rights 
to about 70% of the water diverted from Mill Creek, which 
it also uses for agricultural purposes , and Peyten Pacific 
holds water rights to an unspecified amount of Mill Creek 
flows.  The State Water Resources Control Board 
(“SWRCB”) is an agency that regulates water rights for all 
of California .  Defendants Esquivel, D’Adamo, Maguire, 
Firestone, and Morgan are members of the SWRCB , and 
defendants Ekdahl and Sobeck are its officers. 
In 2014 and 2015, in response to drought conditions, 
Defendants and their predecessors adopted emergency 
regulations curtailing “nearly all off -stream diversions on 
Mill, Deer, and Antelope Creeks.”  After California issued 
 
1 In a concurrently filed memorandum disposition, we affirm the district 
court’s dismissal of Plaintiffs’ takings claims. 
6 LOS MOLINOS MUTUAL WATER CO. V. EKDAHL 
an emergency drought proclamation in May 2021, 
instructing the SWRCB to evaluate the minimum instream 
flow required to protect fish, the SWRCB again adopted 
emergency regulations and curtailment orders. 
On September 1, 2021, the SWRCB issued a Notice of 
Opportunity for Public Comment on draft emergency 
regulation for Mill and Deer Creeks , with comments due 
within a week.   At a regularly scheduled meeting three 
weeks later , in which Plaintiffs participated to the extent 
allowed, Defendants issued a year -long resolution that 
adopted a revised version of the draft emergency regulation.  
The resolution emphasized the importance of Mill and Deer 
Creeks to salmon and steelhead migration and determined 
that any  water diversion that “would cause or threaten to 
cause flows to fall beneath the draught emergency minimum 
flows” was an “unreasonable use” of water. 
Authorized by the resolution, in October 2021, 
Defendant Ekdahl  issued curtailment orders for  Deer and 
Mill Creeks to meet the minimum flow targets set under the 
emergency regulation, ordering the twenty-two water rights 
holders on those creeks  to reduce or stop diverting water.  
Plaintiffs allege, and Defendants do not dispute, that only the 
water rights holders on Mill and Deer Creeks were subjected 
to the 2021 emergency regulation and curtailment orders.  
The curtailment orders established a $1,000 daily penalty for 
violations and a $2,500 penalty for every acre-foot diverted. 
Plaintiffs sought reconsideration of the curtailment 
orders, but their requests were denied.  The  curtailment 
orders were in effect for eight months.  Plaintiffs allege that 
the emergency regulation and curtailment orders prevented 
them “from exercising their vested water rights,” requiring 
them “to bypass all or substantially all of the flows of Deer 
 LOS MOLINOS MUTUAL WATER CO. V. EKDAHL 7 
Creek and Mill Creek”  that they ordinarily diverted for 
agricultural purposes. 
A similar process occurred in 2022.  On August 5, 2022, 
the SWRCB issued a notice that it planned to readopt 
emergency regulations and set a comment deadline of 
August 11.  Five days after the deadline, the emergency 
regulations were readopted.  New curtailment orders 
followed.  Plaintiffs again requested and again were denied 
reconsideration.  Like the 2021 curtailment orders, the 2022 
curtailment orders lasted eight months. 
Plaintiffs allege that, in both 2021 and 2022, they 
requested and were denied evidentiary hearings and the 
opportunity to cross -examine the SWRCB and California 
Department of Fish and Wildlife (“CDFW”) employees who 
testified in favor of the emergency orders.  Instead, Plaintiffs 
were allowed only five minutes during the public comment 
period at the 2021 meeting.
2 
In October 2021, Plaintiffs sued in federal district court, 
raising, among others, procedural due process claims under 
the Fourteenth Amendment and takings claims under the 
Fifth Amendment , and seeking injunctive and declaratory 
relief prohibiting Defendants from adopting or enforcing 
similar “emergency regulations and/or curtailment orders 
without holding a due process evidentiary hearing and 
without payment of just compensation for the taking of real 
property and real property rights .”  The district court 
dismissed the procedural due process claim s, concluding 
that the emergency regulations and curtailment orders were 
“legislative” and not “adjudicat ory,” so no evidentiary 
 
2 Plaintiffs’ allegations do not indicate to what extent they were allowed 
to participate in the 2022 meeting. 
8 LOS MOLINOS MUTUAL WATER CO. V. EKDAHL 
hearing was required.  It also dismissed the takings claims as 
barred by Eleventh Amendment sovereign immunity.  
Concluding that Plaintiffs’ request for declaratory relief rose 
or fell with their procedural due process and takings claims, 
the district court also found Plaintiffs ineligible for 
declaratory relief.  Plaintiffs voluntarily dismissed their 
remaining claims, and timely appealed. 
II. Jurisdiction and Standard of Review 
We have jurisdiction to review the district court’s final 
dismissal order under 28 U.S.C. § 1291.  “ We review de 
novo a district court’s order granting a motion to dismiss for 
failure to state a claim.”  Depot, Inc. v. Caring for 
Montanans, Inc., 915 F.3d 643, 652 ( 9th Cir. 2019).  
Dismissal should be affirmed “where there is no cognizable 
legal theory or an absence of sufficient facts alleged to 
support a cognizable legal theory.”  Id. (citation omitted).  At 
the motion -to-dismiss stage, “ we accept as true all well-
pleaded factual allegations,” but “are not required to accept 
as true legal conclusions couched as factual allegations.”  
Parents for Priv. v. Barr , 949 F.3d 1210, 1221 ( 9th Cir. 
2020) (citation omitted). 
III. Discussion 
A. 
As a threshold matter, we must determine whether we 
have jurisdiction.  This court lacks jurisdiction to hear moot 
claims.  Feldman v. Bomar , 518 F.3d 637, 642 (9th Cir. 
2008).  An action is moot when “the issues presented are no 
longer live and … the parties lack a legally cognizable 
interest” in a remedy.  Alaska Ctr. f or Env’t v. U.S. Forest 
Serv., 189 F.3d 851, 854 (9th Cir. 1999).

leads.caseName: Matthew O'Donnell v. Loudoun County School Board
leads.text:
COURT OF APPEALS OF VIRGINIA 
Record No. 2181-25-4 
MATTHEW O’DONNELL 
v. 
LOUDOUN COUNTY SCHOOL BOARD 
Present: Judges Malveaux, Raphael and Senior Judge Annunziata 
Argued at Fairfax, Virginia 
Opinion Issued November 24, 2026 
FROM THE CIRCUIT COURT OF LOUDOUN COUNTY 
Thomas D. Horne, Judge Designate 
Debra K. Rose (WhitbeckBeglis, PLLC, on briefs), for appellant. 
John F. Cafferky (Jakob T. Stalnaker; Blankingship & Keith, P.C., on brief), for appellee. 
PUBLISHED OPINION BY 
JUDGE MARY BENNETT MALVEAUX 
 Matthew O’Donnell appeals from an order of the circuit court sustaining the demurrer of the 
Loudoun County School Board (“School Board”) and dismissing his petition for judicial review of 
the School Board’s action renaming two public schools. O’Donnell argues the circuit court erred in 
finding that he lacked standing to pursue his petition under Code § 22.1-87. For the reasons that 
follow, we affirm the circuit court. 
I. BACKGROUND 
The School Board Action and O’Donnell’s Petition for Review 
 On October 25, 2022, the School Board revised its School Board Policy 6510 (“Policy 
6510”) to provide procedures for the School Board to “initiate or consider requests to rename an 
existing school facility, at [the School Board’s] discretion.” The same day, the School Board 
 - 2 - 
initiated a “school name review” of two such facilities: Mercer Middle School and Reid 
Elementary School. Following the review and additional proceedings in summer 2024, the 
School Board appointed renaming committees for Mercer Middle and Reid Elementary. 
 The Mercer Middle School renaming committee met three times between October 2024 
and December 2024 and the Reid Elementary School renaming committee met four times 
between October 2024 and January 2025. At each meeting, “[o]pportunity for public comment 
was offered” and audio recordings of the meetings later were posted to the Loudoun County 
Public Schools website. During this time, Loudoun County Public Schools also conducted 
public surveys “to receive additional community feedback and potential [new] name 
suggestions.” On December 19, 2024 and January 8, 2025, respectively, the Mercer Middle and 
Reid Elementary renaming committees voted to recommend renaming those schools and 
provided new name recommendations to the School Board. 
 The School Board conducted a dedicated public hearing on the proposed renaming of the 
two schools on April 9, 2025. It then voted on April 22, 2025 to rename the facilities Gum 
Spring Middle School and Mildred and Richard Loving Elementary School. 
 On May 20, 2025, O’Donnell, the father of a student at the renamed Loving Elementary 
School, filed a petition in the circuit court seeking judicial review of the School Board’s 
renaming actions. See Code § 22.1-87 (providing for circuit court review of school board actions 
upon a petition by a parent, custodian, or legal guardian of a pupil who is “aggrieved” by such 
actions). In his petition, O’Donnell contended that the School Board acted “arbitrarily and 
capriciously” when it voted to rename the two schools “without having complied with the 
requirements of Policy 6510.”1 He alleged that renaming the schools without proper compliance 

1 O’Donnell alleged the School Board failed to adhere to Policy 6510’s procedural 
requirements by: renaming the schools in the absence of written requests for the name changes 
made “in consultation with . . . representing School Board member(s)”; initiating the renaming 

 - 3 - 
with School Board policy produced harm because “[w]hen government bodies violate their own 
policies, it damages public confidence in their integrity and effectiveness.” The failure to follow 
the School Board’s own policies also “harm[ed] students . . . who, according to [the School 
Board’s] Strategic Plan for Excellence, ‘are at the center of all we do.’” O’Donnell specifically 
asserted that his “child . . . has and will continue to be negatively impacted by [the School 
Board’s] actions to rename her school in violation of its own policies and contrary to the 
majority of survey participants” because “[h]er trust in the school system and its leadership has 
been eroded.” He also noted that there would be financial costs associated with renaming the 
two schools, which would “have a financial impact on [him], as a resident and taxpayer in 
Loudoun County.” O’Donnell requested the circuit court find that the School Board acted 
arbitrarily and capriciously and set aside the School Board’s renaming actions. 
The School Board’s Demurrer and Further Proceedings in the Circuit Court 
 The School Board filed a demurrer and plea in bar in response to O’Donnell’s petition. 
In its demurrer, the School Board argued, among other things, that O’Donnell lacked standing to 
petition for judicial review under Code § 22.1-87 because he was “not aggrieved of the School 
Board’s decisions.” This was so, the School Board contended, because O’Donnell did not plead 
any injuries unique to him and distinguishable from those to the general public. In its plea in bar, 
the School Board argued that O’Donnell’s petition was time-barred. 

process without first holding a community town hall; “fail[ing] to appoint all required members 
to the renaming committee[s]”; making reasonable efforts to inform relatives of the schools’ 
current namesakes “of the proposed name change[s] and provid[ing] them with an opportunity to 
address the committee[s]”; failing to consider the results of the public surveys; and failing to 
engage an unbiased, “independent third-party source” to research the renaming options submitted 
to the School Board. 
O’Donnell also alleged the School Board “took steps to prevent the public from having 
access to the public records related” to the renaming process by, among other things, denying his 
VFOIA request for such records. Any alleged VFOIA violation is not at issue in this appeal. 
 - 4 - 
 In a memorandum in opposition to the demurrer, O’Donnell argued that he did have 
standing under Code § 22.1-87 because his “injury . . . is not one that could be shared with any 
[other] member of the public.” He characterized his petition as “[s]imilar to challenges” to 
school board actions on “school facility use, educational programs, and subject matter text 
books,” asserting a “personal interest in the [renaming] process” based on being “aggrieved by 
the fact that he and his daughter must be confronted with the result of the [School Board’s] 
deliberate actions to violate Policy 6510.” 
 The circuit court conducted a hearing on the School Board’s demurrer and plea in bar. At 
the hearing, O’Donnell argued he had pleaded sufficient facts to establish standing because he 
and his daughter were “personally impacted on a daily basis by the name change and have a 
personal stake in the outcome of this action. . . . [W]e have a student who is aggrieved by . . . the 
decision to name the school something else, something they disagree with, and disagree with 
how that decision came about.” O’Donnell contended that “[a] name change in a school’s name 
permeates the entire school culture” because the name is “embedded into curriculum, on 
behavior.” He analogized the present matter as “very similar” to school boundary cases where “a 
big group of students . . . are affected by a boundary decision and those students all ha[ve] 
standing.” 
 Considering the School Board’s standing argument, the circuit court asked counsel for 
the School Board for an example of someone who would have standing under the statute as a 
person aggrieved by the renaming of a school. Counsel replied that the descendants of someone 
who had donated the land for a facility that was then named for them would “have a unique 
interest that, at least arguably, could be implicated.” The circuit court took the matter under 
advisement. 
 - 5 - 
 On September 2, 2025, the circuit court issued a memorandum opinion sustaining the 
School Board’s demurrer. The circuit court noted its obligation to accept as true all the facts 
alleged by O’Donnell and accord him all reasonable inferences that could be drawn from those 
facts. Yet “[d]espite this deferential standard . . . which [O’Donnell’s] claim is accorded on 
demurrer,” the circuit court found that O’Donnell lacked standing to pursue his claim 
challenging the School Board’s renaming actions. Relying primarily on Lafferty v. School Board 
of Fairfax County, 293 Va. 354 (2017), the circuit court held that to pursue his claims under 
Code § 22.1-87, O’Donnell, “as a result of the actions of the [School] Board,[] must have been 
denied some personal or property right distinct from that of the public in general[]. Merely 
having a child in the school district does not provide a basis for standing.” Noting that “[a] 
school naming decision . . . affects the public in general,” the circuit court concluded that 
O’Donnell had “failed to show, by allegation or argument, [that] having to ‘be confronted with 
the result of [the School Board’s] deliberate actions to violate Policy 6510’ burdens him any 
differently from the public generally.”2 
 The circuit court memorialized its ruling in a September 17, 2025 order sustaining the 
School Board’s demurrer and dismissing O’Donnell’s petition. This appeal followed. 
II. ANALYSIS 
O’Donnell argues the circuit court erred in sustaining the School Board’s demurrer 
because it misapplied the term “aggrieved” as it appears in Code § 22.1-87. He further contends 
the circuit court erred by failing to accept as true the factual allegations pleaded in his petition 
and to interpret those allegations in the light most favorable to him. 

2 The circuit court also held that in light of its ruling on the demurrer, “the issue raised by 
the [School Board’s] Plea in Bar need not be addressed.” 
 - 6 - 
“A circuit court’s decision sustaining a demurrer presents a question of law that is 
reviewed de novo on appeal.” Historic Alexandria Found. v. City of Alexandria, 299 Va. 694, 
696 (2021) (citing EMAC, L.L.C. v. County of Hanover, 291 Va. 13, 20 (2016)). Likewise, 
“[i]ssues related to the interpretation of statutes . . . also are questions of law subject to de novo 
review.” Berry v. Bd. of Supervisors, 302 Va. 114, 127 (2023). 
A. The Term “Aggrieved” Under Code § 22.1-87 
“Code § 22.1-87 authorizes a private right of action as a judicial remedy to school board 
actions, allowing parties ‘aggrieved’ by a decision of the [b]oard to challenge the action in circuit 
court within 30 days.” Lafferty, 293 Va. at 362. Specifically, the statute provides that “[a]ny 
parent, custodian, or legal guardian of a pupil attending the public schools in a school division 
who is aggrieved by an action of the school board may . . . petition the circuit court having 
jurisdiction in the school division to review the action of the school board.” Code § 22.1-87. 
Here, addressing the threshold question of standing to pursue judicial review under the statute, 
the circuit court held that to be “aggrieved” under Code § 22.1-87, a school board’s action “must 
have . . . denied [the petitioner] some personal or property right distinct from that of the public in 
general[].” That is, the action of the school board must have “burden[ed]” the petitioner 
“differently from the public generally.”3 O’Donnell argues that in applying this definition of the 
term “aggrieved,” the circuit court defined the term “so narrowly that the types of school board 
action for which parents could have standing under . . . Code § 22.1-87 would be limited in 
contradiction to the plain language of the statute, the intent of the General Assembly in adopting 
it, and applicable case law.” 

3 The circuit court also held that “[m]erely having a child in the school district does not 
provide a basis for standing.” Because O’Donnell never argued in the circuit court that his 
daughter’s mere enrollment in the public schools was sufficient to confer standin

Modified and Affirmed in Part, and Reversed and Rendered in Part and 
Memorandum Opinion filed November 24, 2026. 

In The 

Fourteenth Court of Appeals 

NO. 14-25-00222-CV 

DAVID CLARY, MARIO PEREZ, THE CLARY GROUP LLC AND 
RIDGELINE RENEWABLES, LLC, Appellants 
V. 
GREYCO PERSONNEL SERVICES, LLC F/K/A GREYCO SEISMIC 
PERSONNEL SERVICES, LLC, Appellee 

On Appeal from the 133rd District Court 
Harris County, Texas 
Trial Court Cause No. 2018-07540 

MEMORANDUM OPINION 

By four issues on appeal, appellants challenge the trial court’s judgment 
against them under the Texas Uniform Trade Secrets Act (“TUTSA”). We reverse 
and render a take -nothing judgment in favor of Ridgeline Renewables, LLC 1 

1 In the record and in this memorandum opinion, Ridgeline Renewables, LLC is sometimes 
referred to as “Ridgeline Renewables” or “Ridgeline.” 

2 

because it was only found liable on a theory of civil conspiracy. Because the 
evidence was legally sufficient to support the trial court’s judgment against 
appellants David Clary, Mario Perez, and The Clary Group LLC (“The Clary 
Group”), and because Greyco Personnel Services, LLC (“Greyco”) prevailed on its 
TUTSA claim, we affirm the trial court’s final judgment against Clary, Perez, and 
The Clary Group. However, we modify the final judgment against Clary, Perez, and 
The Clary Group to delete joint and several liability which was not supported by a 
proportionate-responsibility finding or other legal basis for joint and several liability. 
I. Factual and Procedural Background 
Greyco sued appellants alleging various causes of action including breach of 
contract and misappropriation of trade secrets. During the six- week trial, the jury 
heard from fifteen witnesses. These witnesses included appellants Clary and Perez, 
as well as Greyco’s corporate representative , Franklin Fallon. Each of these three 
witnesses offered testimony that spanned multiple days at trial. Greyco’s former co-
owners Paul Mitcham and Marcus Pullicono also testified, along with plaintiff and 
defense damages experts. In addition to the testimony presented at trial, several 
defense exhibits and over a thousand Greyco exhibits were admitted into evidence. 
These exhibits included emails, crew lists, payroll records, financial records, and 
invoices. In relevant part, the evidence at trial showed the following facts. 
Greyco is a staffing company that provides personnel services to the solar -
energy market. Perez was a trusted employee who maintained Greyco’s worker 
roster and supervised workers in the field. Greyco hired Clary and his company 
Medgrow Marketing, LLC, later renamed The Clary Group, to provide marketing 
services for less than one year. Clary requested a Greyco email address and title, 
and had access to Greyco customers, internal financial information, pay scales, and 
other materials. 
3 

Before and after Greyco ended its relationship with Clary and his company, 
Clary established a competing business. As Clary built the competing business, 
Perez transmitted Greyco information to him. Perez emailed Greyco documents to 
his own personal email, including worker lists, qualifications, project experience, 
and drug-test records. Perez remained Greyco’s personnel director for nine months 
while Clary simultaneously described Perez as the personnel head for Clary’s new 
business. During that period, Perez identified Greyco workers for Clary who might 
be available for Clary’s projects. 
When Perez left Greyco, he returned a phone that had been wiped of data. 
Greyco’s examination of Perez’s laptop showed that he had emailed the “Mario 
Matrix,” a compilation of Greyco employee data, to his personal email account. 
Greyco presented evidence that its personnel were its principal asset and that 
employee recruitment, training, testing, skills, experience, time sheets and related 
data were confidential trade secrets. Greyco also treated customer contact lists as 
secret and restricted access to its Master Service Agreement (“MSA”) and other 
confidential information through secure servers. 
Greyco Owner Paul Mitcham’s Testimony 
Paul Mitcham owns Greyco and has worked in oil and gas since 1984. 
Mitcham helped form Greyco in 2010 after identifying demand for personnel 
services in seismic exploration. Mitcham testified Greyco’s personnel value derived 
from workers it trained, vetted, and organized into compatible teams for remote, 
difficult assignments. Greyco used worker rosters, qualifications, costing sheets, 
customer lists, MSAs, supplements, and time sheets in its staffing business. 
Greyco entered solar work in 2015 after completing a small, profitable 
Louisiana solar carport project with fewer than fifteen workers. Based on this 
4 

experience, Greyco pivoted to its business to solar because seismic work was 
slowing. Greyco then sought remote, crew-based solar work for its existing labor 
force. 
Marcus Pullicino introduced David Clary as a salesman and negotiated 
Greyco’s arrangement with him. Greyco retained Clary as an independent contractor 
to develop solar business. Mitcham testified that Clary initially lacked knowledge 
of solar staffing and remote crew-based labor. Greyco showed Clary costing sheets, 
MSAs, supplements, time sheets, employee lists, customer lists, employee ratings, 
and worker rosters. According to Mitcham , Greyco relied on the confidentiality 
provision in Clary’s signed contract with Greyco when providing that information. 
Greyco sought to protect employee rosters, costing methods, customer lists, 
employee ratings, and access to top performers. Mitcham conceded that Greyco 
employee names were displayed on an office chalkboard visible to persons inside 
the office. 
Mitcham testified that Greyco became concerned in August 2016 when they 
learned that Clary had stopped copying Greyco on his emails with customers, and 
that he had made disparaging remarks about Greyco. By the end of 2016, Clary no 
longer worked for Greyco. 
Mitcham described Mario Perez as Greyco’s field supervisor, an integral 
employee, and a good, hardworking “Mr. Fixit.” Perez trained and recruited 
workers, coordinated drug tests, organized personal protective equipment, placed 
crews, and identified workers who worked well together. Perez was valuable to 
Greyco, responsive to problems, and well- liked by clients and coworkers. A 
September 2016 sales report stated crews performed twenty to twenty-five percent 
better when Perez was present. The report stated that the client wanted Perez to 
remain through the project. 
5 

Greyco Co-Founder Marcus Pullicino’s Testimony 
Marcus Pullicino co-founded Greyco in 2010, was a minority owner and chief 
operating officer. Pullicino testified he helped build Greyco from a startup into a 
major land- seismic labor provider. Pullicino testified that staffing companies 
require substantial upfront capital for vehicles, insurance, payroll, office space, legal 
costs, and transportation. Pullicino left Greyco by the end of 2016. 
Pullicino identified Greyco’s personnel as its principal competitive asset. 
Greyco maintained employee databases on secure servers with controlled access and 
login requirements. Greyco provided trained remote labor, transportation, lodging, 
and crew logistics for large projects. Pullicino testified that Greyco workers could 
collect unemployment and work elsewhere between Greyco projects. Workers 
received no pay during periods when Greyco had no projects. Greyco entered the 
solar market around 2015 because seismic activity declined and solar projects used 
similar remote labor. The solar transition allowed Greyco to retain its labor force, 
and Mario Perez became a leading Greyco supervisor. 
Pullicino recruited his longtime friend David Clary around 2015 to help 
develop Greyco’s solar business. Pullicino provided Clary customer lists, market 
research, sales templates, and industry materials because Clary lacked solar and 
staffing experience. Pullicino understood Greyco’s agreement with Clary was that 
Greyco owned confidential information Clary developed or compiled while working 
for Greyco. Pullicino also understood Greyco’s employee conflict-of -interest 
provision to prohibit employees working for competitors during Greyco 
employment. 
Greyco time sheets recorded employee names, work dates, positions, and start 
and end times. Greyco provided time sheets to clients under confidentiality 
agreements. Hourly employees could work elsewhere between Greyco projects and 
6 

were not barred from working for competitors during those time periods. Seismic 
and solar work involved different tasks, although workers could become trained 
solar operators through solar experience. 
Pullicino considered Greyco’s operating methods and MSA proprietary and 
confidential as a whole, despite seeing many MSAs during his career. Pullicino 
agreed MSAs resulted from negotiations and either party could supply one. 
Pullicino identified an April 2016 email in which Clary circulated Greyco’s MSA in 
an email, showing Clary had possession of the MSA. 
Greyco Operations Director Fallon Franklin’s Testimony 
Fallon Franklin testified that she was Greyco’s director of operations and had 
previously served as its assistant controller . Franklin also identified herself as 
Greyco’s custodian of records and corporate representative. Franklin estimated that 
Perez induced at least 100 Greyco workers to leave and work for Clary or one of his 
companies. Franklin identified three individuals who were hired by Clary on or 
about November 13, 2017, while they were still working on Greyco’s SunEnergy1 
project. Franklin testified further that Perez provided Clary with experienced 
Greyco personnel who had already been vetted and had undergone drug testing at 
Greyco’s expense—a process that cost Greyco substantial time and money. Franklin 
testified that Clary had pricing information and access to Greyco’s personnel. 
Clary’s Testimony 
David Clary testified that he entered the solar industry through business-
development work for Greyco beginning in October 2015, researching the market, 
developing its renewable -energy strategy, and helping secure early solar projects. 
Clary described himself as an independent contractor, although he used a Greyco 
email address and business cards identifying him as a Greyco vice president. 
7 

Clary testified that he later formed and solely owned The Clary Group, 
operated Ridgeline Renewables as a d/b/a, then began Ridgeline’s labor business in 
July 2017, and subsequently formed other affiliated entities. Clary admitted that he 
used a blank Greyco MSA as a template but denied using Greyco’s pricing, time 
sheets, workforce matrix, handbook, or other documents. 
Clary testified that he knew Mario Perez through Greyco and began 
communicating with him about solar projects by at least June 2017, while Perez 
remained a Greyco employee. Clary contacted Perez because he had a solar-project 
opportunity and knew Perez “knew some guys,” asking whether Perez knew anyone 
who was unemployed and wanted work. Perez subsequently reported that workers 
were interested, and Clary directed him to relay when and where they should meet 
after Clary arranged transportation, protective equipment, and a hotel onboarding 
location. Perez also suggested his sister, Angel, as a translator for Spanish-speaking 
workers at the onboarding session. Clary minimized Perez’s early role, describing 
him as a friend and informal “helper,” denying that Perez recruited, onboarded, 
managed, or advanced funds to Ridgeline employees except insofar as he assisted 
Angel. 
Clary testified that Perez formally joined The Clary Group d/b/a Ridgeline 
Renewables on December 1, 2017, eventually serving as director of operations and 
project superintendent. Clary later identified Perez as Ridgeline’s superintendent. 
In that operational role, Perez recruited workers, supervised crew le

leads.caseName: Gloria v. Salinas v. Howard A. Lang Junior
leads.text:
Reversed and remanded and Opinion filed November 24, 2026. 
 
 
 
In The 
 
Fourteenth Court of Appeals 
  
NO. 14-25-00255-CV 
 
GLORIA  V. SALINAS, Appellant 
V. 
HOWARD  A. LANG JUNIOR, Appellee 
 
On Appeal from the 80th District Court 
Harris County, Texas 
Trial Court Cause No. 2022-38621 
 
OPINION 
 
This dispute concerns residential property at 4931 Michael Drive in Harris 
County purchased for $47,500 and the attendant payment obligation.  In the 
plaintiff’s view after 20 years  she had overpaid by some amount . From t he 
defendant’s view she had paid up to 97% , leaving her owing somewhere between 
$5,401.32 to $8,047.67.  She sued for what could only be a relatively small amount 
compared to the judgment assessed against her. This spurred in motion a series of 
events such that she  went unrepresented during high- stakes summary -judgment 
2 
 
proceedings and lost.  Attorneys’ fees totaling $45,000 were assessed against her.   
We reverse and remand.   
I. FACTUAL AND PROCEDURAL BACKGROUND 
On November 18, 2006, Plaintiff -Appellant Gl oria Salinas assumed the 
purchaser’s rights and obligations to Defendant -Appellee Howard Lang under an 
April 30, 2001 contract for deed.  The contract reflected a $40,000 principal 
balance, ten -percent annual interest, and 240 monthly principal-and -interest 
payments, plus escrow payments for taxes and insurance.  The seller retained title 
until all amounts due were paid and then was required to provide a general 
warranty deed.  
The parties dispute whether Salinas satisfied her payment obligations.  
Salinas contends that she paid more than $130,000 and satisfied the debt on March 
2, 2020, about fifteen months before the May 31, 2021 maturity date.  Salinas 
contends that she continued paying because she was unaware whether the debt had 
been satisfied.   Salinas also contends that Lang failed to credit some payments, 
misapplied principal payments, and increased the number of remaining payments 
shown on annual statements without her consent .  Lang maintains that Salinas 
frequently paid late, incurred late fees, stopped paying in November 2021, and 
owed a balance at maturity.    
The Lawsuit 
Salinas sued Lang on June 28, 2022, alleging that she had paid the contract 
in full; Lang answered and counterclaimed, alleging that she had not.  Salinas’s 
live pleading included claims for breach of contract, trespass -to-try-title, and 
executory-contract claims.  Lang’s counterclaim was for breach of contract.
1   
 
1 Based on Lang’ s calculation, Salinas had satisfied about 97% of her payment 
3 
 
Lang filed a hybrid traditional and no-evidence motion for summary 
judgment in May 2023 on Salinas’s contract and Property Code claims, and on his 
breach-of-contract counterclaim.  Salinas responded and filed supporting evidence, 
but the motion was passed and never considered by the court.   
On September 23, 2024, Lang later filed another similar motion, his “Motion 
for Partial and No- Evidence Summary Judgment,” which is the impetus for this 
appeal.  While there is no notice of submission or notice of oral hearing in the file, 
the parties do not dispute that the motion was set for oral hearing on November, 
11, 2024, which the record indicates in fact occurred.   After Lang’s dispositive 
motion was filed but before the hearing and before Salinas’s response was due, the 
trial court granted Salinas’s counsel’s motion to withdraw on October 22, 2024.  At 
the November 11 hearing, Salinas appeared on her own behalf and told the court 
she received notice of the order granting her counsel’s withdrawal on November 5, 
six days before the summary-judgment hearing.  The court disputed her account of 
late notice by reference to  information on file that Salinas’s attorneys had 
contacted her of their withdrawal.  Salinas had filed her response on the eve of the 
hearing along with various responsive exhibits; no affidavit or declaration was 
provided to authenticate many of the exhibits which were not self -authenticating 
documents.  
At the November 11 hearing, the trial court, implicitly satisfied that Lang ’s 
motion stood firmly on its own— conclusively addressing all elements ( but the 
damage element ) of his breach of contract counter -claim an d sufficiently 
identifying elements of all of Salinas’s claims—announced it was ruling by default 
and granted Lang’s motion on account of Salina’s untimely response:  
THE COURT: Okay. So, unfortunately, the rules apply to everyone in 
 
obligation.  
4 
 
this courtroom the same, and because there was no response on file 
timely to Defendant’s motion, as a matter of law, I grant Defendant’ s 
motion.2 
The same day the court signed an order granting Lang’s summary -judgment 
motion. However, contrary to the court’s in-court statements, among the court’s 
recitals were its consideration of “ Plaintiff’s response (if any), .  . .and all 
admissible and competent evidence on file.” 
After a bench trial on attorney’ s fees, on December 27, 2024, the court 
issued its final judgment, awarding Lang $5,401.32 in actual damages on his 
breach of contract claim, prejudgment interest, $45,000 in attorney’s fees, and 
conditional appellate attorney’s fees.  
During the litigation, Lang delivered  an executed and notarized general 
warranty deed and a $2,000 c heck to Salinas ’s attorney.  Though Salinas rejected 
the check, she asks that we take judicial notice she recorded the deed on April 11, 
2025 (four days after she filed her notice of appeal).   
II.
 ISSUES AND ANALYSIS 
On appeal, Salinas challenges the trial court’s summary judgment order as to 
her claims for declaratory relief concerning title, breach of contract, trespass to try 
title, and violations of the Executory Contract for Conveyance Act, as well as 
Lang’s breach-of-contract counterclaim.  
A. Standard of review and applicable law 
Standard of Review 
Lang’s summary-judgment motion was a hybrid, combining a no- evidence 
 
2 Immediately after this announcement the court admonished Salinas to speak with an 
attorney, and discussed setting the trial date for what remained, which Lang’ s attorney described 
as “our damage issue, which is our attorney’s fees, and the amount she overpaid.” 
5 
 
motion with a traditional motion for summary judgment. We review both 
traditional and no- evidence summary judgments de novo. See Boerjan v. 
Rodriguez, 436 S.W.3d 307, 310 (Tex. 2014) (per curiam). 
Summary Judgments 
In the partial traditional summary judgment component of his hybrid motion, 
Lang sought summary judgment on liability for his breach -of-contract 
counterclaim against Salinas, wi th damages—including reasonable and necessary 
attorneys’ fees—to be determined at trial.  To obtain a traditional summary 
judgment, the movant must produce evidence showing that no genuine issue of 
material fact exists and that it is entitled to judgment as a matter of law. See Town 
of Shady Shores v. Swanson, 590 S.W.3d 544, 551 (Tex. 2019). If the movant 
produces evidence conclusively establishing its right to summary judgment, then 
the burden of proof shifts to the non- movant to present grounds for avoiding 
summary judgment, including evidence sufficient to raise a genuine issue of 
material fact, if the non-movant so contends. Wyrick v. Bus. Bank of Tex., N.A. , 
577 S.W.3d 336, 346 (Tex. App. —Houston [14th Dist.] 2019, no pet.).  The 
nonmovant may raise a genuine issue of material fact by producing more than a 
scintilla of evidence establishing the existence of the challenged element. Town of 
Shady Shores, 590 S.W.3d at 551. 
In the no -evidence component of his motion, Lang moved to dismiss 
Salinas’s claims for trespass to try title, breach of contract, and violations of the 
Executory Contract for Conveyance Act.
3 In a no -evidence motion for summary 
judgment, the movant asserts that there is no evidence of one or more essential 
 
3 Although not challenged by this appeal, Lang also challenged Salinas ’s claims for 
violations of the Texas Deceptive Trade Practices Act, violations of the Texas Debt Collection 
Act, violations of the Texas Fraud in Real Estate and Stock Transactions Act, and statutory and 
common-law usury. 
6 
 
elements of the claim or defense for which the nonmovant bears the burden of 
proof at trial. Tex. R. Civ. P. 166a(i); see Timpte Indus., Inc. v. Gish, 286 S.W.3d 
306, 310 (Tex. 2009). The burden then shifts to the nonmovant to present evidence 
raising a genuine issue of material fact as  to the elements specified in the motion. 
See Mack Trucks, Inc. v. Tamez, 206 S.W.3d 572, 582 (Tex. 2006). We will affirm 
a no -evidence summary judgment when (a) there is a complete absence of 
evidence of a vital fact, (b) the court is barred by rules of law or of evidence from 
giving weight to the only evidence offered to prove a vital fact, (c) the evidence 
offered to prove a vital fact is no more than a mere scintilla, or (d) the evidence 
conclusively establishes the opposite of the vital fact. See City of Keller v. Wilson, 
168 S.W.3d 802, 816 (Tex. 2005). 
Executory Contracts 
An executory contract, or a “contract for deed,” is a real-estate transaction 
that allows the seller of the property to retain title until the purchaser has paid for 
the property in full. Flores v. Millennium Interests, Ltd. , 185 S.W.3d 427, 429 
(Tex. 2005); Bryant v. Cady , 445 S.W.3d 815, 819 (Tex. App. —Texarkana 2014, 
no pet.) (“An executory contract for real property typically results in the buyer 
being entitled to immediate posses sion of the property on the making of a down 
payment.”). “A contract for deed differs from a conventional contract for the sale 
of realty, in which the seller and purchaser mutually agree to complete payment 
and title transfer on a date certain at which time the purchaser generally obtains 
both title and possession.” Bryant , 445 S.W.3d at 819; Graves v. Diehl, 958 
S.W.2d 468, 471 (Tex. App. —Houston [14th Dist.] 1997, no pet.) (noting that 
under contract for deed, title remains with seller until purchase price is paid in full, 
which typically occurs in installments over course of years). A contract for deed 
“serves to provide persons unable to obtain conventional mortgage financing an 
7 
 
alternative means of purchasing real property.” Shook v. Walden, 368 S.W.3d 604, 
625 (Tex. App.—Austin 2012, pet. denied); Ferrara v. Nutt, 555 S.W.3d 227, 236 
(Tex. App.—Houston [1st Dist.] 2018, no pet.). 
Texas Property Code Chapter 5, Subchapter D governs certain executory 
contracts for the conveyance of real property. See Tex. Prop. Code Ann. §§ 5.061–
.086; Smith v. Davis , 462 S.W.3d 604, 609 (Tex. App. —Tyler 2015, pet. denied) 
(stating that executory contracts for residential properties are “highly regulated by 
the legislature”). Subchapter D imposes several procedural requirements, including 
notice and disclosure requirements, remedies upon default, and the purchaser ’s 
right to cancel the contract. See, e.g., Tex. Prop. Code Ann. §§ 5.063, .064, .069, 
.071, .074; Morton v. Nguyen, 412 S.W.3d 506, 510 (Tex. 2013). Section 5.077 
requires an executory-contract seller to furnish the purchaser each January —
postmarked by January 31 if mailed— with an annual accounting stating the 
amounts paid and owed, the number of remaining payments, specified tax and 
insurance information, and any required accounting of insurance proceeds, and it 
imposes liquidated damages and reasonable attorney’s fees for noncompliance, 
with the obligation continuing after the purchaser obtains title. Tex. Prop. Code 
Ann. § 5.077.  Section 5.079 treats a recorded executory contract as a deed with a 
vendor’s lien for the unpaid contract price, implies a general warranty unless the 
contract limits it, and— if the contract has neither been recorded nor converted 
under Section 5.081 —requires the seller to transfer recorded legal title to the 
purchaser within 30 days after receiving fi
