NOTICE 
This slip opinion is subject to formal revision before it is published in an 
advance sheet of the Ohio Official Reports.  Readers are requested to 
promptly notify the Reporter of Decisions, Supreme Court of Ohio, 65 
South Front Street, Columbus, Ohio 43215, of any typographical or other 
formal errors in the opinion, in order that corrections may be made before 
the opinion is published. 
 
 
SLIP OPINION NO. 2026-OHIO-4626 
CLEVELAND METROPOLITAN BAR ASSOCIATION v. WILSON. 
[Until this opinion appears in the Ohio Official Reports advance sheets, it 
may be cited as Cleveland Metro. Bar Assn. v. Wilson, Slip Opinion No.  
2026-Ohio-4626.] 
Attorneys—Misconduct—Violations of the Rules of Professional Conduct, 
including neglecting several clients’ legal matters, providing incompetent 
representation, making false statements to two tribunals, making frivolous 
arguments on behalf of one client, failing to cooperate in one disciplinary 
investigation, engaging in conduct prejudicial to the administration of 
justice, and engaging in conduct adversely reflecting on fitness to practice 
law—Indefinite suspension. 
(No. 2026-0724—Submitted August 4, 2026—Decided November 24, 2026.) 
ON CERTIFIED REPORT by the Board of Professional Conduct of the Supreme 
Court, No. 2025-016. 
__________________ 
SUPREME COURT OF OHIO 
 2 
The per curiam opinion below was joined by KENNEDY, C.J., and FISCHER, 
DEWINE, BRUNNER, DETERS, HAWKINS, and SHANAHAN, JJ. 
 
Per Curiam. 
{¶ 1} Respondent, Arleesha Shawntay Wilson , of Cleveland, Ohio, 
Attorney Registration No. 0097351, was admitted to the practice of law in Ohio in 
2018. 
{¶ 2} In a five-count December 2025 second amended complaint, relator, 
the Cleveland Metropolitan Bar Association, charged Wilson with 18 violations of 
the Rules of Professional Conduct .  Relator alleged that, among other things , 
Wilson had neglected several clients’ legal matters, provid ed incompetent 
representation, made false statements to two tribunals , made frivolous arguments 
on behalf of one client by citing four cases that do not exist and twice 
misrepresenting the legal significance of seven other cases, and failed to cooperate 
in one of the resulting disciplinary investigations.  Relator further alleged that 
Wilson had engaged in conduct that was prejudicial to the administration of justice 
and adversely reflected on her fitness to practice law. 
{¶ 3} The parties entered into stipulations of fact , misconduct, and 
aggravating and mitigating factors.  They also stipulated to the amount of restitution 
that Wilson owes in connection with her misconduct and submitted 157 stipulated 
exhibits.  Wilson was the only witness to testify at the hearing before a three -
member panel of the Board of Professional Conduct.   Relator argued that Wilson 
should be indefinitely suspended from the practice of law for her misconduct, while 
Wilson urged the board to allow her to continue practicing law.  Although the panel 
chair gave the parties the opportunity to submit posthearing briefs to support their 
proposed sanctions, Wilson did not file a brief. 
{¶ 4} After the disciplinary hearing, the panel issued a report , finding by 
clear and convincing evidence that Wilson had committed the charged misconduct.  
January Term, 2026 
 3 
The panel adopted the parties’ stipulated aggravating and mitigating factors.  Two 
panel members recommended that Wilson be suspended from the practice of law 
for two years with one year conditionally stayed and that she be required to serve a 
one-year period of monitored probation upon her reinstatement to the practice of 
law.  The third panel member dissented, stating that he would indefinitely suspend 
Wilson from the practice of law.   The board adopted the panel’s findings of fact  
and conclusions of law but recommended that Wilson be indefinitely suspended 
from the practice of law.  No objections have been filed. 
{¶ 5} For the reasons that follow, we  adopt the board’s findings of 
misconduct and indefinitely suspend Wilson from the practice of law in Ohio. 
I.  FINDINGS OF FACT 
A.  Count One: The Cameron Matter 
{¶ 6} In November 2020, Wilson agreed to represent Dana Huddleston -
Cameron and De rrick L. Cameron in a breach -of-contract case that their former 
counsel had filed on their behalf against 1st Choice Roofing Company in the 
Cuyahoga County Court of Common Pleas , case No. CV-20-929626.  The case 
involved a contract for repairs and replacement of the roof of a commercial building 
owned by the Camerons .  Wilson did not carry professional-liability insurance at 
the time and failed to inform the Camerons of that fact in writing as required by 
Prof.Cond.R. 1.4(c). 
{¶ 7} Wilson filed a notice of appearance in the Camerons ’ case on 
November 11, 2020.  Although 1st Choice had sent discovery requests, including 
requests for information regarding the Camerons’ damages, to the Camerons’ 
former counsel in July 2020, the case file that Wilson received from the Camerons’ 
former counsel did not include those requests .  Wilson did not respond to any 
discovery requests, and she told the trial court at an August 2022 hearing that she 
had no knowledge of the requests sent by 1st Choice before she was retained. 
SUPREME COURT OF OHIO 
 4 
{¶ 8} On July 12, 2021, the trial court held a settlement conference.  During 
that conference, Wilson informed the court that the Camerons had hired a new 
roofing contractor to replace the roof at a cost of $202,250 .  The court noted that 
the figure was significantly higher than 1st Choice’s original contract price of 
$95,000 and was different from the ranges stated in the expert report provided by 
the Camerons’ former counsel .  Wilson stated that she did not recall see ing an 
expert report and that she was unfamiliar with the issue of potential warranty 
coverage under the original contract.  The court instructed the parties to familiarize 
themselves with the case  and indicated that another settlement conference would 
be scheduled. 
{¶ 9} During a status conference held later in July, the trial court, at the 
request of 1st Choice, instructed Wilson to inform the Camerons to stop all work 
on the roof.  Wilson represented to the court that the Camerons would cease all 
work and allow 1st Choice an opportunity to inspect the roof before a new roof was 
installed.  Although 1st Choice sent a cease-and-desist letter to Wilson on the same 
day as the status conference, work on the roof continued and was completed in fall 
2021, and 1st Choice was deprived of an opportunity to inspect the roof before it 
was replaced.  The Camerons eventually stated under oath that they were unaware 
that 1st Choice had requested that they cease work on the roof and give 1st Choice 
an opportunity to inspect it. 
{¶ 10} Wilson also failed to cooperate with 1st Choice’s efforts to schedule 
the Camerons’ depositions.  She simply did not reply to the first three attempts at 
scheduling by 1st Choice.  After a fourth inquiry, Wilson discussed with opposing 
counsel’s paralegal that December 8, 2021, may be a possible date to conduct the 
depositions, but she did not respond to further efforts  by opposing counsel to 
confirm that date.  Consequently, on December 7, 1st Choice moved to extend the 
case deadlines because it had not yet had the opportunity to depose the Camerons 
or inspect the roof. 
January Term, 2026 
 5 
{¶ 11} Wilson sought and obtained leave to file an amended complaint  on 
the Camerons’ behalf.  Wilson filed the amended complaint on February 15, 2022, 
and 1st Choice filed a mot ion to dismiss it; Wilson failed to  oppose the motion.  
The trial court dismissed all claims except the breach -of-contract claim and set 
August 31 as the trial date. 
{¶ 12} On the day of the trial, the trial court discussed potential settlement 
with the parties.  During that discussion, the court learned that Wilson had provided 
1st Choice with a copy of the new roofing contractor’s contract for and photographs 
of the new roof but that she had not produced any bills or invoices for the new roof.  
Counsel for 1st Choice requested dismissal of the case with prejudice as a discovery 
sanction, while Wilson requested a continuance so that she could  produce 
responsive documents.  The court was not inclined to continue the trial and warned 
Wilson t hat if the case was continued, it would order the Camerons to pay 1st 
Choice’s legal fees related to Wilson’s failure to supplement discovery.  The court 
further advised Wilson that if the case moved forward, it would grant an adverse-
inference instruction based on the Camerons’ failure to permit 1st Choice to inspect 
the roof before it was replaced.  When Wilson informed the court that the Camerons 
would dismiss the case under Civ.R. 41(A) and then refil e it, the court reminded 
Wilson that 1 st Choice would still be entitled to both the adverse -inference 
instruction based on the spoliation of evidence and the fees it had incurred because 
of her failure to supplement discovery. 
{¶ 13} After Wilson filed a notice of voluntary dismissal of the case on the 
Camerons’ behalf and the trial court dismissed the case without prejudice , 1 st 
Choice filed a motion for sanctions for frivolous conduct under Civ.R. 11 and R.C. 
2323.51.  Wilson filed objections to the motion on the Camerons’ behalf , and the 
court scheduled a hearing on the motion for December 7, 2022.  On December 2, 
the court’s staff attorney emailed counsel for both parties, informing them that the 
December 7 hearing needed to be rescheduled, providing a list of potential dates  
SUPREME COURT OF OHIO 
 6 
for the hearing , and asking counsel to confer with their clients and select a new 
date.  Wilson discussed the potential dates with Huddleston -Cameron, who 
informed her that the dates would not work, but Wilson never responded to the staff 
attorney’s email.  The court set the hearing for January 17, 2023. 
{¶ 14} On January 9, Wilson filed a motion to continue the hearing based 
on a scheduling conflict and the Camerons’ need for additional time to secure 
transportation from their out-of-state home.  The trial court denied the motion .  
Wilson appeared at the hearing without the Camerons.  She informed the court that 
she had never agreed to the January 17 hearing date.  When asked why she had not 
informed the court of the conflict when she first discovered it, Wilson claimed that 
she had responded to the staff attorney’s email but that the hearing was scheduled 
anyway.  The court instructed Wilson to locate her responsive email, which she 
found in her draft s folder; the email  had never been sent.  The draft email she 
showed the court bore the date of the hearin g, though at her disciplinary hearing, 
Wilson testified that the date automatically updated whenever she opened the draft. 
{¶ 15} The Camerons refiled their lawsuit against 1st Choice on August 30, 
2023.  The trial court dismissed the Camerons’ refiled lawsuit with prejudice in 
February 2024. 
{¶ 16} On November 20, 2023, the trial court ordered Wilson to pay a 
sanction of $13,155.50 to Thomas Connick, counsel for 1st Choice, within 60 days 
of the court’s order.  The amount represented the reasonable attorney fees that 1 st 
Choice had incurred as a result of Wilson’s failure to supplement discovery and her 
failure to comply with the court’s orders.  Wilson did not comply with the court’s 
sanctions order or respond to Connick’s repeated requests for payment.  
Consequently, the court ordered Wilson to appear and show cause why she had 
failed to comply with the court’s sanctions order.  On July 22, 2024, the court found 
Wilson in contempt of

Thomas v. Doba
ROBERT J. THOMAS ET AL. v. FRAN
DOBA ET AL.
(AC 47816)
Moll, Suarez and Clark, Js.*
Syllabus
The defendants, the town of Bethany and its tax collector and B Co., the suc-
cessful bidder at a town tax sale, appealed and the plaintiff property owners 
cross appealed from the trial court’s judgment as to liability, rendered before 
the court conducted a hearing in damages, invalidating the property deed 
issued by the tax collector to B Co. and quieting title to the property at issue 
in favor of the plaintiffs after it had been sold at the tax sale. At oral argu-
ment before this court, the municipal defendants and the plaintiffs contended 
that both appeals were taken from a final judgment pursuant to Ledyard v. 
WMS Gaming, Inc. (330 Conn. 75) because the only damages sought by the 
plaintiffs were attorney’s fees and, in supplemental memoranda ordered by 
this court, all parties agreed that the trial court’s decision constituted a final 
judgment notwithstanding that the trial court had not yet entered orders 
concerning amounts owed pursuant to statute (§ 12-159a). Held:
This court dismissed the appeals for lack of subject matter jurisdiction, 
as the trial court’s decision did not constitute a final judgment in light of 
that court’s failure to make the required orders as to amounts owed under 
§ 12-159a subsequent to the tax sale.
Argued February 11—officially released November 24, 2026
Procedural History
Action to recover damages for, inter alia, the alleged 
negligence of the named defendant et al., and for other 
relief, brought to the Superior Court in the judicial 
district of New Haven, where BTL Enterprise, LLC, 
was cited in as a party defendant; thereafter, the case 
was tried to the court, Hon. Juliett L. Crawford, judge 
trial referee; judgment in part for the plaintiffs, from 
which the defendants appealed, and the plaintiffs cross 
appealed to this court. Appeals dismissed.
Melinda A. Powell, for the appellants-cross appellees 
(named defendant et al.).
*The listing of judges reflects their seniority status on this court as 
of the date of oral argument.
Thomas v. Doba
David L. Weiss, for the appellant-cross appellee (defen-
dant BTL Enterprise, LLC).
Joshua A. Winnick, for the appellees-cross appellants 
(plaintiffs).
Opinion
CLARK, J. The defendants, Fran Doba, the town of 
Bethany (town and, together with Doba, municipal defen-
dants), and BTL Enterprise, LLC (BTL), appeal, and the 
plaintiffs, Robert J. Thomas and Susan S. Thomas, cross 
appeal from the judgment of the trial court invalidat-
ing a tax collector’s deed and quieting title to certain 
real property in favor of the plaintiffs. The dispositive 
issue in these appeals is whether they must be dismissed 
for lack of a final judgment because the judgment from 
which the parties have appealed does not include certain 
orders required by General Statutes § 12-159a1 concern-
ing the amount that the plaintiffs are required to pay 
BTL, the successful bidder at the tax sale, for taxes, 
1General Statutes § 12-159a provides: “(a) In any action brought to 
prove the invalidity of a collector’s deed or enjoin tax sale proceedings, 
other than an action based on fraud, the court shall, if the complaining 
party is successful, order the complaining party to pay to the tax collector 
or to the person or persons claiming an interest pursuant to such deed, 
(1) amounts representing taxes, interest and other charges lawfully due 
from the complaining party at the time of such tax sale with interest 
from the date of such tax sale at the rate provided in section 12-157, 
and (2) the reasonable costs of payment of taxes, insurance premiums, 
repairs, maintenance and demolition of any structures constituting a 
nuisance, and the fair market value of any capital improvements made 
to the property by such persons, with interest at the rate provided in sec-
tion 37-3a computed from the time of such expenditure or improvement.
“(b) Any person entitled to payments pursuant to subsection (a) of 
this section shall, upon the recording of a certificate of judgment lien, 
be entitled to a lien on such property. The priority of such lien shall be, 
in the case of the amounts described in subdivision (1) of said subsec -
tion (a), prior to all other interests except taxes, and, in the case of the 
amounts described in subdivision (2) of said subsection (a), such priority 
as rules of law and principles of equity provide.
“(c) Nothing in subsection (a) of this section shall prohibit the court 
from awarding the complaining party any damages which may be proven. 
Any damages awarded shall be reduced by the amounts described in 
said subsection (a).”
Thomas v. Doba
insurance, and other costs associated with maintain-
ing the property since the date of the sale. We conclude 
that the appeals were not taken from a final judgment 
and, accordingly, dismiss the appeals for lack of subject 
matter jurisdiction.
The following facts and procedural history are rel-
evant to our resolution of these appeals. In 1997, the 
plaintiffs acquired title to certain real property located 
at 43 Bethany Farms Road in Bethany (property). On 
June 2, 2017, Doba, the town’s tax collector, issued a 
bill to the plaintiffs for taxes due for the October 1, 2016 
grand list. The taxes were due in two equal installments 
on July 1, 2017, and January 1, 2018, and considered 
delinquent if not paid by the first of the month follow-
ing the installment due date. The plaintiffs did not pay 
either installment by the delinquency date.
Between November 2017 and June 2018, Doba made 
several unsuccessful attempts to collect the delinquent 
taxes from the plaintiffs, including by sending mul-
tiple written demands and issuing a property alias tax 
warrant.2 On July 9 and August 7, 2018, Doba sent the 
plaintiffs notices informing them that a tax sale would 
be held on September 28, 2018, if they failed to pay all 
outstanding taxes, interest, fees, and other charges. 
Both notices listed the total amount due as of the end 
of the month preceding the notice, and instructed the 
plaintiffs that additional amounts would continue to 
accrue and to contact Attorney John D. Watts, whom 
the town had retained in connection with the tax sale, 
for the payoff amount.
On August 28, 2018, the plaintiffs, without contact-
ing Watts to obtain the payoff amount, made a pay-
ment through the town’s online portal in the amount 
of $24,157.77. Because the online portal did not include 
an option to pay attorney’s fees and costs, however, the 
plaintiffs’ payment did not include the fees and costs that 
had accrued as of the date of the payment. By letter dated 
August 29, 2018, Watts notified the plaintiffs that the 
2See General Statutes (Rev. to 2017) § 12-162.
Thomas v. Doba
town would be returning their payment because it did 
not include the total amount due and instructed them to 
contact his office to obtain the payoff amount in order to 
stop the tax sale. On September 4, 2018, Doba sent the 
plaintiffs a third notice informing them that the tax sale 
was still scheduled for September 28, 2018, and would 
proceed unless the plaintiffs paid the total amount of 
the outstanding taxes, interest, fees, and other charges. 
The plaintiffs did not make any additional payments.
On September 28, 2018, Doba conducted the tax sale, 
at which BTL purchased the property for $38,000. On 
October 4, 2018, Doba sent the plaintiffs a notice inform-
ing them that the property had been sold to BTL, that 
they had until March 28, 2019, to redeem the property 
and that, if they failed to do so, the plaintiffs’ title to the 
property would be extinguished. A copy of the notice was 
also served on the plaintiffs by a state marshal on October 
23, 2018. The plaintiffs failed to redeem the property 
by the redemption date, and the deed vesting title to the 
property in BTL was recorded on April 2, 2019.
The plaintiffs commenced the present action on Sep-
tember 3, 2019. The operative complaint, filed on August 
24, 2020, asserts counts sounding in negligence and neg-
ligence per se against the municipal defendants; reckless-
ness against Doba; a claim for indemnification against 
the town; a claim seeking to invalidate the tax collector’s 
deed; a claim seeking to quiet title to the property; and a 
claim seeking a declaratory judgment that the town was 
bound to accept the plaintiffs’ August 28, 2018 online 
payment as satisfaction for the total amount due.
A court trial was held on November 28 through 30, 
2023, before the court, Hon. Juliett L. Crawford, judge 
trial referee. During the trial, the plaintiffs presented 
evidence concerning, inter alia, the amount of attorney’s 
fees they had paid to prosecute this action and to defend 
a separate summary process action brought by BTL.3 
3BTL filed the summary process action on June 25, 2019, but that 
action was stayed by agreement of the parties pending resolution of 
the present case.
Thomas v. Doba
In their posttrial brief to the trial court, the plaintiffs 
argued that, with respect to the count of their complaint 
seeking to invalidate the deed, they were entitled to 
“damages” in the form of attorney’s fees they incurred 
prosecuting the present case and defending the summary 
process action.
On June 27, 2024, the trial court issued a memoran-
dum of decision finding in favor of the plaintiffs on all 
counts of the complaint except the count asserting a 
recklessness claim against Doba. The court determined 
that the deed was invalid on the ground that “[t]he plain-

Matter of People v Commons W., LLC 
 2026 NY Slip Op 06932

 Court of Appeals

 In the Matter of the People & c.
by Letitia James, & c., Appellant, 
 v 
 Commons West, LLC, et al., Respondents. 

 Decided on November 23, 2026 
 No. 86 

 Patrick A. Woods, for appellant. 
 Curtis A. Johnson, for respondents. 
 Safe Horizon, Inc. et al., American Civil Liberties Union et al., CNY Fair Housing, Inc. et al., National Housing Law Project et al., Housing Works et al., amici curiae. 

 [*1] 
 Order reversed, with costs, and respondents' motion to dismiss the proceeding and cross-motion for summary judgment on their counterclaim for declaratory relief denied. Chief Judge Wilson and Judges Singas, Troutman and Halligan concur, Chief Judge Wilson in a concurring opinion, in which Judges Troutman and Halligan concur and Judge Singas in a separate concurring opinion. Judge Garcia dissents and votes to affirm in an opinion, in which Judges Rivera and Cannataro concur. 
 Decided November 23, 2026 
 Wilson, Chief Judge (Concurring):

 The New York State Human Rights Law (HRL) prohibits landlords from discriminating against tenants based on their source of income. The federal Section 8 program provides housing assistance to needy persons. Several landlords in Tompkins County challenge the HRL as facially unconstitutional — although the HRL itself says nothing about searches or inspections — because federal law requires inspections of rental properties as part of the Section 8 program. The landlords contend that the HRL is facially unconstitutional because they cannot refuse tenants on the basis of their receipt of Section 8 vouchers, and are thus forced to submit to inspections of their properties, books and records in violation of the Fourth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution. Because the HRL itself contains no search requirement and, even if the State and Federal laws could somehow be treated as a single statute, the combination would not be unlawful in every application, we hold that the HRL is not facially unconstitutional. 
 I. 
 Fifty years ago, Congress passed the Housing and Community Development Act of 1974, amending the U.S. Housing Act of 1937 by adding a housing choice voucher program—now commonly referred to as Section 8. The Section 8 program aims to help "low-income families in obtaining a decent place to live" and to "promot[e] economically mixed housing" (42 USC § 1437f [a]). Public housing agencies (PHAs)—which may be state, county, or local agencies—administer the program pursuant to guidance from the United States Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD), which also funds the program (42 USC § 1437a [b] [6]; 24 CFR. 982.51). HUD provides qualifying Section 8 beneficiaries with assistance payments in the form of vouchers that they may use to pay rent, cover homeownership expenses, or buy a home (42 US.C §§ 1437f [o], 1437f [y]). 
 Section 8 obliges participating landlords to sign a Housing Assistance Payments (HAP) contract with a PHA (42 USC § 1437f [c] [8]). HUD sets the HAP contract terms (24 CFR 982.451 [a] [1]). The present HAP contract requires landlords to grant the PHA access to the property and provide access to any relevant records. Section 8 also requires PHAs to inspect rental units for safety and habitability once before a renter can receive vouchers to pay for that property, biennially thereafter, and additionally in response to complaints (42 USC § 1437f [o] [8]). Despite the language in the HAP contracts regarding landlord consent, no statutory provision mandates the PHA rely on landlord consent to conduct inspections, nor does any statutory provision mandate inspection of landlord records. 
 In 2019, New York amended the HRL, making it illegal for landlords to discriminate against prospective renters based on their source of income. The Legislature enacted that change to combat widespread behavior by landlords rejecting tenants for their use of assistance vouchers (New York State Division of Budget, Mem. in Support of Fiscal Year 2020 Exec. Budget, Educ., Labor, and Family Assistance Art. VII Legislation, 24.1). Executive Law § 296(5)(a) provides: 
 "5. (a) It shall be an unlawful discriminatory practice for the owner, lessee, sub-lessee, assignee, or managing agent of, or other person having the right to sell, rent or lease a housing accommodation, constructed or to be constructed, or any agent or employee thereof: (1) To refuse to sell, rent, lease or otherwise to deny to or withhold from any person or group of persons such a housing accommodation [*3] because of the . . . lawful source of income . . . of such person or persons, or to represent that any housing accommodation or land is not available for inspection, sale, rental or lease when in fact it is so available." 
 Executive Law § 292(36) defines "lawful source of income" to include: 
 "income derived from . . . any form of federal, state, or local public assistance or housing assistance including, but not limited to, section 8 vouchers, or any other form of housing assistance payment or credit whether or not such income or credit is paid or attributed directly to a landlord, and any other forms of lawful income. The provisions of this subdivision shall not be construed to prohibit the use of criteria or qualifications of eligibility for the sale, rental, leasing or occupancy of publicly-assisted housing accommodations where such criteria or qualifications are required to comply with federal or state law, or are necessary to obtain the benefits of a federal or state program." 
 In 2020, two prospective tenants filed complaints with the Attorney General, asserting that the respondent landlord owners of certain residential rental properties in Tompkins County had refused to rent apartments to them because they intended to pay with Section 8 vouchers. The Attorney General began this proceeding under Executive Law § 63 (12), alleging that the landlords' refusal violated Executive Law § 296 (5) (a) (1). The Attorney General sought an injunction compelling the landlords to design and implement nondiscriminatory housing accommodation policies regarding sources of income, set aside a percentage of units in each of their buildings for Section 8 recipients for three years, undergo court monitoring and pay restitution and civil penalties. 
 The landlords moved to dismiss the petition on several grounds and brought a cross-claim seeking declaratory relief. The relevant ground here is their contention that the HRL has the effect of compelling them to participate in the Section 8 program if an otherwise qualified prospective tenant applies to rent an apartment with Section 8 income. Then, because the required federally prescribed HAP contract requires the landlords to consent to searches, the landlords are being subjected to warrantless inspections of property and records in violation of the Fourth Amendment. Tompkins County Supreme Court agreed and dismissed the Attorney General's petition; it held that Executive Law § 296(5)(a)(1) was "unconstitutional to the extent that it makes it an unlawful discriminatory practice to refuse to rent or lease housing accommodations to any person, or group of persons, because their source of income includes Section 8 vouchers" ( People by James v Commons W., LLC , 80 Misc 3d 447, 452 [Sup Ct, Tompkins County 2023]). 
 Following the dismissal, the local PHA responsible for administering the Section 8 program in Tompkins County published a guidance document that directed the agency either to seek consent from the tenant or to procure an administrative warrant to conduct any inspections if a landlord objected. The Attorney General then moved to renew her opposition to respondents' motion to dismiss, and the landlords cross-moved for summary judgment. Supreme Court denied the Attorney General's renewal motion and granted the cross-motion, declaring the HRL facially unconstitutional. Relying on our decision in Sokolov v Village of Freeport (52 NY2d 341 [1981]), Supreme Court held the source-of-income law "facially unconstitutional because it compels a property owner to [*4] provide advance consent to such searches in violation of the Fourth Amendment" ( People by James v Commons W., LLC , 85 Misc 3d 1055, 1057 [Sup Ct, Tompkins County 2024]). 
 On the Attorney General's appeal, the Appellate Division affirmed, agreeing the proceeding was properly dismissed and defendant was entitled to a declaration in its favor ( People v Commons W., LLC , 252 AD3d 190, 192 [3d Dept 2026]). Also relying on Sokolov , the court held that "although the source-of-income discrimination law does not, itself, require any searches, [the landlords] are indirectly compelled through the terms of the Section 8 program and the HAP contract" to consent to warrantless searches ( id . at 196). The Attorney General appealed to this Court as of right. 
 II. 
 As a threshold matter, the Attorney General challenges the landlords' constitutional claim as nonjusticiable. She argues that the alleged harm is too speculative to support a claim because the enforcement action brought by the State does not presently threaten respondents' Fourth Amendment rights. 
 "The function of the courts is to determine controversies between litigants. They do not give advisory opinions" ( Self-Insurer's Assn. v State Indus. Commn. , 224 NY 13, 16 [1918, Cardozo, J.] [internal citations omitted]). "The 'justiciable controversy' upon which a declaratory judgment may be rendered requires not only that the plaintiffs in such an action have an interest sufficient to constitute standing to maintain the action but also that the controversy involve present, rather than hypothetical, contingent or remote, prejudice to plaintiffs" (American Ins. Assn. v Chu , 64 NY2d 379, 383 [1985]). State justiciability is distinct from the federal standing doctrine, and New York has no analogous case or controversy requirement ( People v Johnson , 46 NY3d 65, 74 [2025]). Under our caselaw, "[t]he existence of an injury in fact . . . ensures that the party seeking review" has a sufficiently "concrete interest" to make the action "capable of judicial resolution" ( Society of Plastics Indus. v County of Suffolk , 77 NY2d 761, 772 [1991] [internal quotation marks omitted]). "To constitute an injury in fact, [a party's] claimed harm must be direct and immediate such that it cannot be prevented or significantly ameliorated by administrative action or by steps available to the complaining party" ( Matter of Acevedo v New York State Dept. of Motor Vehs. , 29 NY3d 202, 218 [2017]). "[S]tanding rules should not be applied in an overly restrictive manner where the result would be to completely shield a particular action from judicial review" ( Matter of Stevens v New York State Div. of Criminal Justice Servs. , 40 NY3d 505, 515 [2023]). 
 Here, no one has conducted any warrantless inspections, nor are any on the immediate horizon. But the present suit arose out of the State's prosecution of the landlords for noncompliance with the HRL. The State's enforcement action presents the landlords with a sufficiently direct and immediate harm to render the cross-claim justiciable. 
 III. 
 The landlords' central claim is that the New York Human Rights Law is facially unconstitutional because "it is impossible for landlords to comply with the [law] without signing a HAP contract consenting to [warrantless] searches" in violation of their Fourth Amendment rights. 
 Statutes are presumptively constitutional; "courts strike them down only as a last unavoidable result after every reasonable mode of reconciliation of the statute with the Constitution . . . has been found impossible" ( Stefanik v Hochul , 43 NY3d 49, 57 [2024] [internal quotation [*5] marks omitted]). C

Lease has an end date of 2033 and contains a quiet enjoyment 
provision stating that: “Lessee shall peaceably hold and enjoy 
said premises for the term hereby demised without hinderance or 
interruption by Lessors or any other person or persons lawfully 
claiming by, through or under them except as herein expressly 
provided.”  The Lease does not include any reference to Kewalo 
Lane being on the Lease premises or that the lessee is obligated 
to provide access to and from Kamehameha Highway for any nearby 
kuleana owners.  
Between May 2011 and February 2012, KS submitted to 
HTC seven lease extension proposals (referred to as LOIs) to 
extend the Lease to 2067-68.  The LOIs also proposed jointly 
creating a “New Lane,” with HTC contributing its thirty-foot 
*** FOR PUBLICATION IN WEST’S HAWAI‘I REPORTS AND PACIFIC REPORTER *** 
 
6 
 
wide driveway and KS contributing a ten-foot wide strip from its 
thirty-foot wide historic Kewalo Lane, to benefit the HSL 
project and kuleana owners, including the Wards, and to increase 
customer traffic for both HSL and HTC shopping centers.  The 
First Amended Complaint alleges that a February 17, 2012 LOI was 
acceptable to HTC, except for one provision.  The First Amended

  In the meantime, in 2011, KS obtained a final 
environmental assessment (EA) for the HSL project from the DPP,

  On May 29, 2012, KS informed HTC that KS was

New Lane.  HTC asserts it repeatedly urged KS to extend the

Instead, the First Amended Complaint alleges KS, in bad faith

  Rather than the New Lane access for the HSL project, 
KS replaced it with a mid-block access (Mid-Block Lane) that did 
not provide proper fire apparatus access, i.e. emergency access,

7 
 
to the kuleana owners behind the HSL lot.  Instead of 
constructing the New Lane, KS obscured that it would build over

  KS pursued permitting and tentative subdivision 
approval for the HSL project.  There are extensive allegations 
in the First Amended Complaint regarding documents between KS 
representatives and DPP about the permit approval process.  Some 
documents correctly reflect Kewalo Lane being part of the HSL 
project property, but other documents improperly reflect that 
Kewalo Lane was on HTC’s property.  
In 2014, as part of the HSL project, KS built a 
restaurant on a portion of historic Kewalo Lane, and in doing 
so, used large parts of HTC’s driveway during its construction 
operations, against HTC’s repeated objections.  As a result:  
HTC submitted plans to KS and the City to construct a fence 
to prevent [KS’s] HSL [project] construction activities on 
HTC’s property and to prevent [the] HSL [project] – which

and consultants, HTC removed the emergency access gates 
from the plans. 
 
The First Amended Complaint details communications 
about the construction activities by KS on HTC’s property and 
apparently related discussions about the location of Kewalo

8 
 
Lane.  These communications included: written confirmation from 
KS’s attorney to HTC’s lawyers that Kewalo Lane is not located 
on HTC’s leased premises and that access for the kuleana owners 
“is a KS issue, not an HTC issue”; and a representation in 
writing from KS’s land manager to DPP that Kewalo Lane is not on 
HTC property.   
KS’s efforts to obtain permitting and tentative 
subdivision approval for the HSL project included constructing 
the new Mid-Block Lane.  The First Amended Complaint alleges 
that in seeking its tentative subdivision approval, KS

In December 2015, DPP issued tentative subdivision

the final survey map including the deletion of the 30 ft.

1 
 
               2026 IL App (5th) 250085 
                         NO. 5-25-0085 
                              IN THE 
       APPELLATE COURT OF ILLINOIS 
FIFTH DISTRICT 
______________________________________________________________________________ 
 
THE CITY OF MATTOON,    ) Appe al from the 
       ) Circuit Court of 
 Plaintiff-Appellee,    ) Coles County. 
       ) 
v.       ) No. 18- OV-164 
       )  
TIM L. QUACKENBUSH,    ) Honorable 
       ) Mark E. Bovard, 
 Defendant-Appellant.    ) Judge, presiding. 
______________________________________________________________________________ 
 
 JUSTICE SHOLAR delivered the judgment of the court, with opinion. 
 Presiding Justice Cates concurred in the judgment and opinion. 
 Justice Barberis concurred in part and dissented in part, with opinion. 
 
 OPINION 
¶ 1 In this appeal, defendant , Tim L. Quackenbush, contends that the circuit court of Coles 
County erred when the court imposed $53,000 in fines for ongoing violations of the public 
nuisance ordinance found in the Mattoon City Code . Specifically, he alleges that the City of 
Mattoon did not follow the ordinance by filing separate failure to comply citations for the ongoing 
violations. Defendant also argues that the trial court’s decision finding the defendant’s properties 
in violation of the public nuisance ordinance was against the manifest weight of the evidence. For 
the following reasons, we affirm in part and reverse in part. 
¶ 2  I. BACKGROUND 
¶ 3 Defendant is the owner of two parcels of real property, located in the 2100-2400 blocks of

text of this decision may be 
changed or corrected prior to 
the filing of a Petition for 
Rehearing or the disposition of 
the same. 
2 
 
Broadway Avenue in Mattoon, Illinois . One property is located on the north side  of Broadway 
Avenue (North Property), and the other property is located on the south side of Broadway Avenue 
(South Property). On September 12, 2018, the City of Mattoon (City) filed a non-traffic complaint 
against defendant. The complaint alleged that, on September 4, 2018, defendant was in violation 
of two city ordinances. Specifically, the complaint alleged that defendant was in violation of  
(1) section 159.46 of the Mattoon City Code § 159.46 (passed May 5, 2015) (Code) pertaining to 
special use permits ,1 and (2) section 95.02 regarding public nuisances.  Mattoon City Code 
§ 95.02(A) (passed  June 1, 2004). Section 95.02(A) provides as follows: “No person shall erect, 
contrive, cause, continue, maintain or permit to exist any public nuisance within the city.” Id.  
¶ 4 Section 95.01(A) of the Code defines “public nuisance”: 
 “(A) As used in this chapter, a PUBLIC NUISANCE shall mean any act, 
thing, occupation, condition or use of property that shall continue for such length of 
time as to: 
 (1) Substantially annoy, injure or endanger the comfort, health, repose 
or safety of the public; 
 (2) In any way render the public nuisance in life or the use of property; 
 (3) Greatly offend the public morals or decency; or 
 (4) Unlawfully or substantially interfere with, obstruct or tend to obstruct or 
tender dangerous for passage any street, alley, highway, navigable body of water 
or other public way.” Mattoon City Code§ 95.01(A) (passed Sept. 6, 2016). 
 
1The North Property was zoned I ndustrial when purchased by defendant, and the South Property 
was zoned C-4 when purchased by defendant. The City changed the designation of both properties to C -3 
in 2015. The City initially contended that defendant’s continued use of the properties as Industrial and C-4 
required a special use permit. The trial court found that defendant’s use of the properties was grandfathered 
in and that he was not required to have a special use permit. The City did not appeal this finding. 
3 
 
Section 95.01(B) provide d a none xclusive list of 20 “acts, conduct, omissions, conditions or 
things” that are considered nuisances. Mattoon City Code § 95.01(B) (passed Sept. 6, 2016). 
¶ 5 Initially, the matter was continued several times to allow the City and defendant  to work 
toward a resolution. On November 16, 2018, the trial court ordered the City to provide defendant 
with a list of specific issues and violations . The City provided defendant  with the list in a letter 
dated December 10, 2018. Regarding the North Property, the City listed the following “issues and 
violations”:  
“Empty chemical totes; totes storing scrap wood, concrete and debris; a hot tub; 
steel tanks; refrigerators; inoperable vehicles; hundreds of wooden pallets; scrap 
metal of all sorts; plastic  barrels; empty gasoline tanks; scrap wood of all sorts; 
empty rollers for electric cable; scrap plastic; used carpeting; scrap wooden fencing; 
trash containers and roll -offs full of various scrap and debris; steel barrels; wood 
and metal barricades of some sort outside the fence on City owned property.” 
Regarding the South Property, the City listed the following “issues and violations”: 
“Numerous shipping containers used as a fence; dozens of wooden pallets ; scrap 
asphalt; scrap metals of all sorts; masonry and brick scattered about; numerous 
chemical totes with various scrap stored inside; trash roll -off dumpster; steel 
beams; old Wareco gas station roof; inoperable vehicles; scrap wood of all sorts; 
semi-trailer.” 
The letter further noted that the list was not “ ‘all inclusive’ but rather a starting point for violations 
that are alleged regarding City of Mattoon zoning and public nuisance ordinance violations.” 
¶ 6 The matter proceeded to a bench trial on November 22, 2019. Jason Taylor, Police Chief 
for the City, testified that defendant ’s properties had “basically been turned into a junkyard” and 
4 
 
that “[t]here is scrap metal, debris of all sorts. It’s not a viable business entity. It’s simply a scrap 
yard or a junkyard it appears to me.” Taylor said that he spoke with defendant in May 2018 about 
the condition of the properties and followed up with a letter. According to Taylor, defendant  was 
told that the conditions were such that properties were a public nuisance and that he needed to 
clean up his property. Taylor identified photographs from May 2018, showing the conditions on 
the properties, including one where that was “a critter of some sort jumping over a wall.” The 
photographs showed wood pallets, a mattress, chemical totes, a couch, a hot tub, and various pieces 
of metal, including, but not limited to, a dumpster or tr ash can, a safe or a filing cabinet, a metal 
drum, a metal sign , and metal gas tanks. Scattered throughout the properties wa s vegetation in 
excess of the eight inches permissible under the Code. Taylor opined that majority of the materials 
present on the properties was “refuse, garbage or debris.” 
¶ 7 Chief Taylor also testified that defendant  removed, per the City’s request, certain items 
from the c ity-owned alleyway, but that he was using those items to build a wall around the 
property. Part of the property was fenced, and defendant used semi trailers, dozens of empty 
chemical totes, various pieces of wood fencing, and empty oil wells filled with scrap wood to 
create a barrier. Taylor testified that that the Code allows  the owner of properties zoned C -4 and 
Industrial to erect chain link, screening, or privacy fences not to exceed eight feet in height, but 
that erecting such a fence requires a permit. Taylor testified that defendant never sought a permit. 
¶ 8 Regarding the list of violations provided to defendant in December 2018, Chief Taylor 
testified that defendant  had not brought the properties into compliance with the Code. Taylor 
identified a series of photographs of the properties taken on December 21, 2018. The photographs 
showed that the condition of the properties was largely unchanged. Taylor identified a series of 
photos taken in April 2019. The photos again demonstrated that the condition of the property was 
5 
 
largely unchanged. The photos show shipping containers being used for what Taylor characterized 
as a fence, several large steel beams, deteriorating wood, carpeting, a fuel tank, overgrown brush, 
and the roof to an old Wareco gas station. Finally, Taylor identified several photos of the properties 
that were taken in September 2019, which showed little change to the conditions on the property. 
Taylor characterized Defendant’s progress on the property as “close to none.” 
¶ 9 On cross -examination, Chief Taylor was asked about other local businesses, Mervis 
Industries and Harris Metals, which  are also engaged in the scrap metal business. When asked 
what distinguishes those businesses from defendant’s business, Taylor responded that they did not 
involve public nuisances and that they were running “viable business[es].” Taylor acknowledged 
that scrap metal is valued by the pound and that the defendant owns a demolition and excavating 
business. On redirect, Taylor testified that he had not seen any business being operated out of the 
properties and that , although there was a building that could be used as an office, there was no 
indication of any sort of business activity. The City rested. 
¶ 10 Defendant called Matthew Frederick as his first witness. Frederick was employed by the 
City as an electrical planning and zoning official. Frederick testified that the Code allowed 
Industrial and C-4 zoned properties to have a fence, but that a fence was not required. Frederick 
opined that scrap metal and wooden pallets were permissible on industrial property, but the pallets 
could only be there if they were made to withstand the elements . “[O]therwise you’re just going 
to end up [with a] pile of rotten wood.” 
¶ 11 Frederick testified that the north side of the North Property had chain link fencing, but that 
he could not guarantee it r an the whole perimeter. The east side of the North Property had full 
chain link and some privacy fencing. Regarding the south side  of the North Property, Frederick 
testified that he believed the fencing was patchy, but it was full chain link when  the property 
6 
 
operated as a brickyard. With regard to the South P roperty, Frederick testified that the  “fencing 
consists of shipping containers and [sea 2] containers.” On cross-examination, Frederick testified 
that he believed defendant had a small welding shop in one of the buildings on the properties, but 
that he had  not seen a lot of fabrication occurring on the site. He also opined that “ even if 
something” is permissible under a particular zone, it is still subject to the nuisance ordinance. 
¶ 12 Defendant testified that he was the owner of T.Q. Demolition and Excavating, and that they 
tear down buildings, houses , and deep clean at the properties. He had been in the business since 
1978. He bought the North Property in 2012 and the South Property in 1996. He sold salvaged 
metal when the price is up. He also recovered lumber, bricks, and electrical wiring from demolition 
jobs, and he sold those items through the years. Defendant  testified that he  burned wood in the 
winter for heat. Outdoors he used a barrel. He also had a pallet burner that he used to heat his shop.  
¶ 13 Defendant testified that the City hired him to secure the scene of a fire using barriers made 
from some of the plastic totes that he kept on his property. Defendant testified that he had multiple 
uses for the plastic totes: he cut the tops off and filled them with brick to make barricades, and he 
used them for the storage of bulk wood, metal and wire. Some totes were filled with water, because 
the City fire department required him to have water on site, and the site lacked running water. The 
South Property was lined with storage container units around the perimeter.

(west) side had a chain link fence. The south side o

leads.court: New Jersey Superior Court Appellate Division
leads.text:
SUPERIOR COURT OF NEW JERSEY 
 APPELLATE DIVISION 
 DOCKET NO . A-0408-25 

PLANET SHRED RECORDS 
MANAGEMENT LLC and 
PLANET SHRED LLC, 

 Plaintiffs -Appellants, 

v. 

2301 ATLANTIC AVENUE LLC, 
JD COMMERCIAL & 
INDUSTRIAL PROPERTIES, LLC, 
VICTOR P. IORIO, and ROBERT 
MANETTA, 

 Defendants -Respondents. 
______________________ _________ 

Argued October 14, 2026 – Decided November 23, 2026 

Before Judges Natali and Jablonski. 

On appeal from the Superior Court of New Jersey, Law 
Division , Monmouth County, Docket No. L -2574-25. 

Paul H. Appel argued the cause for appellants . 

Timothy P. Beck argued the cause for respondents 
(DiFrancesco Bateman, attorneys; Timothy P. Beck, on 
the brief). 
NOT FOR PUBLICATION WITHOUT THE 
APPROVAL OF THE APPELLATE DIVISION 

This opinion shall not "constitute precedent or be binding upon any court ." Although it is posted on the 
internet , this opinion is binding only on the parties in the case and its use in other cases is limited . R. 1:36 -3. 

2 A-0408 -25 

PER CURIAM 

In this commercial tenancy dispute, Planet Shred Records Management 
LLC, and Planet Shred LLC , appeal from a September 12, 2025 order dismissing 
their complaint with prejudice under Rule 4:6-2(e). The complaint asserted 
claims for declaratory relief, breach of contract, breach of the implied covenant 
of good faith and fair dealing, wrongful eviction, and violations of the New 
Jersey Consumer Fraud Act , N.J.S.A. 56:8 -1 to -229 (the Act) . The court 
concluded those claims were barred by a September 27, 2024 consent judgment 
entered in an earlier landlord -tenant action arising from the identical tenancy 
dispute . Before us, plaintiffs principally reprise the arguments raised before the 
court and maintain that the September 27 consent judgment should not bar their 
subsequent complaint because that judgment was entered under duress and 
economic coercion . 
We are unpersuaded by these arguments and accordingly affirm. As the 
court correctly concluded, t he consent judgment unequivocally operated as an 
accord and satisfaction, consistent with Raji v. Saucedo , 461 N.J. Super. 166, 
171 (App. Div. 2019) , because it resolved the parties ' known claims arising out 
of the tenancy and thereby barred plaintiffs ' subsequent collateral attack of that 
judgment. 

3 A-0408 -25 

Although plaintiffs did not seek relief from the consent judgment by filing 
a Rule 4:50-1 application, that procedural error does not drive our analysis . 
Rather, as we explain, in light of the consent judgment , plaintiffs ' complaint and 
the materials submitted in the motion record do not plead facts sufficient to 
establish duress or economic coercion, a breach of the implied covenant of good 
faith and fair dealing, or a violation under the Act, and repleading would not 
cure those deficiencies . 
Plaintiffs Planet Shred Records Management and Planet Shred operated 
records -management and shredding businesses from a commercial office and 
warehouse space in Wall Township. According to plaintiffs, Planet Shre d 
Record Manageme nt stored hard-copy confidential files for clients including 
attorneys, physicians, and accountants , and Planet Shred shredded documents in 
accordance with their clients ' instructions. 
 Defendants 2301 Atlantic Avenue LLC and JD Commercial & Industrial 
Properties, LLC , owned the property. Plaintiffs alleged defendant Victor P. 
Iorio acted as the property manager and identified defendant Robert Manetta as 
president of Nationwide Imaging Services, Inc., which occupied a substantial 
portion of the building . 

4 A-0408 -25 

In October 2014, Planet Shred Records Management signed a ten -year 
lease commencing February 1, 2015, with two five -year renewal options. For 
more than eight years, plaintiffs maintain ed they paid the same gross rent, and 
defendants accepted those payments without objection. On June 4, 2023, 
plaintiffs received an invoice seeking increased rent based on a September 29, 
2014 email that stated there would be a five -percent rental increase beginning 
in the fourth and seventh years of the lease. The September 2014 email , and the 
email correspondence dated September 30, 2014 with John Cody, president of 
Planet Shred, acknowledging the email, are listed as attachments to the lease. 
After plaintiffs failed to pay the requested rent increases, VP Iorio Realty 
filed a verified complaint in the Special Civil Part, Landlord -Tenant Division in 
August , seeking $101,598.96 in additional rent, late charges, and interest. 
According to p laintiffs , their counsel advised if they unsuccessfully opposed the 
eviction action, VP Iorio could obtain a warrant of removal three days after entry 
of judgment , which would risk displacement of confidential client files if they 
could not be removed prior to the removal proceedings . 
On September 27, 2024, the parties , represented by counsel , negotiated a 
resolution of the tenancy action by way of a consent to enter judgment , under 
which plaintiffs agreed to pay a reduced sum of $51,032.28, while defendants 

5 A-0408 -25 

obtained a judgment for possession with the stipulation that any warrant of 
removal would not be effectuated before April 1, 2025 , thereby permitting 
plaintiff s approximately six months to remove their confidential files from the 
premises . The consent judgment also specified plaintiffs agreed to vacate the 
premises on or before March 31, and defendants would be permitted to show the 
property to prospective tenants on one day 's notice. 
Instead of seeking relief from the court that approved the consent 
judgment by filing an application under Rule 4:50-1, plaintiffs filed this separate 
lawsuit in July 2025, after obtaining the reduced payment obligation and 
extended occupancy provided by th e consent judgment . As noted, they asserted 
five causes of action: (1) declaratory relief seeking an order that the gross rent 
due would not increase for the entire ten -year term ; (2) breach of contract based 
on defendants ' claim for increased rent and improper filing of the landlord -
tenancy action ; (3) breach of the implied duty of good faith and fair dealing; (4) 
wrongful eviction; and (5) a claim under the Act. 
In response, defendants filed a motion to dismiss and they argued 
plaintiffs ' complaint did not assert a ny legally cognizable claim s because by 
entering the consent judgment, the parties entered an accord and satisfaction 
regarding all disputes arising from the tenancy. 

6 A-0408 -25 

Plaintiffs opposed the motion and included the certification of Cody, who 
attested to the facts supporting their duress claims. He explained plaintiffs 
stored approximately 20,000 boxes containing approximately 400,000 hard copy 
files that included confidential records . He maintained if plaintiffs were 
unsuccessful in the eviction action , they would not be able to find and prepare a 
new location or relocate the files and equipment before a ny lockout. He also 
certified their prior counsel advised them that "there are no guarantees in the 
outcome of any litigation, and that if [plaintiffs] opposed the eviction action and 
lost, [the] Landlord could obtain a warrant of removal three days after 
judgment. " He thus contended defendants ' improper tenancy action forced 
plaintiffs to execute the consent judgment as they had no practical choice but to 
agree to vacate and forgo the lease -renewal options . 
Following oral argument s, the trial court dismissed plaintiffs ' complaint 
and entered a conforming order. In its oral decision, the court explained that the 
parties ' prior landlord -tenant matter had been resolved through the consent 
judgment and, relying on Raji, concluded by negotiating and consent ing to a 
pay-and-go agreement , the parties resolve d all differences arising out of the 
tenancy and entered into an accord and satisfaction. Because plaintiffs did not 
assert any violation of rights that are the subject of the pay-and-go agreement , 

7 A-0408 -25 

and because both parties accepted and complied with its terms, the court 
concluded the consent judgment operated as an accord and satisfaction . 
This appeal followed. Before us, plaintiffs raise two main points. First, 
they argue the court committed legal error when it concluded the consent 
judgment constituted an accord and satisfaction and rejected their contention it 
was procured by duress and economic coercion. Second, they maintain the 
complaint pl ed sufficient facts to support their claims for duress and economic 
coercion, breach of the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing, and 
violation under the Act. 
Our review of a dismissal under Rule 4:6-2(e) is plenary. McDermott v. 
Guaranteed Rate, Inc. , 483 N.J. Super. 264, 286 (App. Div. 2025). "[O]ur 
inquiry is limited to examining the legal sufficiency of the facts alleged on the 
face of the complaint " and "plaintiffs are entitled to every reasonable inference. " 
Printing Mart -Morristown v. Sharp Electronics Corp. , 116 N.J. 739, 746 (1989). 
We review "mindful of the test for determining the adequacy of a pleading: 
whether a cause of action is 'suggested ' by the facts. " Printing Mart -Morristown , 
116 N.J. at 746 (quoting Velantzas v. Colgate -Palmolive Co., Inc. , 109 N.J. 189, 
192 (1988)). At this stage, the court is not concerned with the ability of the 
plaintiff to prove the allegations in the complaint. Ibid. 

8 A-0408 -25 

Dismissal is proper when a complaint "states no claim that supports relief, 
and discovery will not give rise to such a claim. " Dimitrakopoulos v. Borrus, 
Goldin, Foley, Vignuolo, Hyman & Stahl, P.C. , 237 N.J. 91, 107 (2019). To 
survive dismissal, a complaint must allege "the essential facts supporting [the] 
plaintiff 's cause of action " but "conclusory allegations are insufficient in that 
regard. " Scheidt v. DRS Techs., Inc. , 424 N.J. Super. 188, 193 (App. Div. 
2012). Thus, dismissal is warranted "where the factual allegations are palpably 
insufficient to support a claim upon which relief can be granted. " Rieder v. 
State, Dep 't of Transp. , 221 N.J. Super. 547, 552 (App. Div. 1987). 
We next address the substantive legal framework governing summary 
dispossess actions, consent judgments, and accord and satisfaction. In general, 
"a summary dispossess action does not permit either a landlord or tenant to plead 
a claim for damages. " Raji, 461 N.J. Super. at 170; Hous. Auth. of Morristown 
v. Little , 135 N.J. 274, 280 (1994). "By confining itself to the landlord 's right 
to possession, and fixing of the amount of rent due to afford the tenant the 
opportunity to avoid eviction by its payment, . . . the statutory summary 
dispossess device provides a quick disposition of the landlord claim for 
possession. " Raji, 461 N.J. Super. at 170 . In a summary dispossess action based 

9 A-0408 -25 

on nonpayment of rent, the claimed amount must be "legal owing. " Housing 
Auth. of Passaic v. Torres , 143 N.J. Super. 231, 236 (App. Div. 1976). 
Once a landlord files an eviction action, the parties may resolve the action 
by entering a consent judgment. A consent judgment "is an agreement that the 
parties desire and expect will be reflected in, and be enforceable as, a judicial 
decree that is subject to the rules generally applicable to other judgments and 
decrees. " DEG, LLC v. Township of Fairfield , 198 N.J. 242, 261 (2009) 
(quoting Rufo v. Inmates of the Suffolk County Jail , 502 U.S. 367, 378 (1992)); 
see also Cmty. Realty Mgmt., Inc. v. Harris , 155 N.J. 212, 226 (1998). A 
consent judgment has "equal adjudicative effect as one entered after trial or other 
judicial determination " and "may only be vacated in accordance with Rule 4:50-
1." Harris, 155 N.J. at 226; Stonehurst at Freeholding v. Township Comm. of 
Freehold , 139 N.J. Super. 311, 313 (Law Div. 1976). 
The essential elements of accord and satisfaction are: (1) "a bona fide 
dispu

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF THE STATE OF NEVADA 

SIEGEL LV NORTH STRIP TOLLESON 
LLC, A NEVADA LIMITED LIABILITY 
COMPANY; SIEGEL LV NORTH STRIP 
MCDOWELL LLC, A NEVADA 
LIMITED LIABILITY COMPANY; 
SIEGEL LV NORTH STRIP 
TROPICANA LLC, A NEVADA 
LIMITED LIABILITY COMPANY; AND 
SIEGEL IN NORTH STRIP SIERRA 
VISTA LLC, A NEVADA LIMITED 
LIABILITY COMPANY, 
Appellants, 
vs. 
EC 215 LAS VEGAS LLC, A 
DELAWARE LIMITED LIABILITY 
COMPANY AND EC 3001 SOUTH LAS 
VEGAS BOULEVARD LLC, A 
DELAWARE LIMITED LIABILITY 
COMPANY, 
Respondents. 
No. 90698 

ORDER OF AFFIRMANCE 

 This is an appeal from a district court order granting a motion for 
a preliminary injunction. Eighth Judicial District Court, Clark County; Susan 
Johnson, Judge. 
 Appellant Siegel LV North Strip Tolleson LLC (Siegel) purchased 
a vacant parking lot on the Las Vegas Strip. Siegel’s property is adjacent to 
respondent EC 215 Las Vegas LLC’s property (Silver City). S ilver City owns 
a strip mall with retail and restaurant tenants. When Siegel purchased the 
parking lot, it did so subject to a Parking Easement Agreement (PEA), which 
grants Silver City and its patrons access to certain portions of Siegel’s parking 
lot. 
 2 
 Siegel put up a chain-link fence around the lot’s perimeter and 
installed gates requiring Silver City’s driving patrons to enter a QR code to 
park for free (hereafter, the “Fence and Gate System”). Siegel’s Fence and Gate 
System effectively cut off pedestrians’ and drivers’ ability to use its parking lot 
as a shortcut to access Silver City’s property. 
 Silver City sued Siegel, a lleging the Fence and Gate System 
violated the PEA, and, as relevant here, moved for a preliminary injunction 
requiring its removal. Following an evidentiary hearing, the district court 
granted the preliminary injunction on July 10, 2024, pending resolution of the 
litigation. The district court denied reconsideration on April 28, 20 25, but 
clarified that Siegel was only required to remove the portion of the Fence and 
Gate System that was subject to the PEA. Siegel appeals. 
 “A preliminary injunction is proper where the moving party can 
demonstrate that it has a reasonable likelihood of success on the merits and 
that, absent a preliminary injunction, it will suffer irreparable harm for which 
compensatory damages would not suffice.” Excellence Cmty. Mgmt. v. Gilmore, 
131 Nev. 347, 350-51, 351 P.3d 720, 722 (2015). We review the district court’s 
decision for an abuse of discretion, id., but review underlying legal issue s, 
including contract interpretation, de novo, Posner v. U.S. Bank Nat’l Ass’n, 140 
Nev. 201, 202, 545 P.3d 1150, 1152 (2024); Farmers Ins. Exch. v. Neal, 119 Nev. 
62, 64, 64 P.3d 472, 473 (2003). 
 Siegel presents two overarching arguments on appeal: (1) the 
district court misinterpreted the PEA as requiring “unobstructed” access to the 
portion of the lot it covers, leading the court to conclude that the Fence and 
Gate System likely violates the PEA; and (2) even if the district court correctly 
interpreted the PEA, the evidence does not support its finding that Silver City 
 3 
would suffer irreparable harm if the Fence and Gate System remained in place 
pending resolution of the litigation. 
The district court did not commit reversible error in determining that Silver 
City’s claims have a likelihood of success on their merits 
 The district court interpreted Section 1.1(a) of the PEA as granting 
Silver City’s patrons the right to unobstructed access to and through the 
Exclusive Easement Parcel, including access to and from Silver City’s property 
and any abutting public streets. Based on that interpretation, the court 
concluded that Silver City was likely to succeed on its claim that the Fence and 
Gate System violated the PEA and ordered Siegel to remove it. 
 Siegel argues that Section 1.1.(a) of the PEA does not grant Silver 
City’s patrons an unobstructed right of access to the parking lot. Alternatively, 
Siegel argues that the district court erroneously relied on Section 1.1(f) because 
that section applies only after Siegel builds a parking garage on the lot. 
Unobstructed access 
 Siegel acknowledges that the PEA gives Silver City’s patrons 
access to Siegel’s parking lot but argues that it does not guarantee 
unobstructed access and therefore permits the Fence and Gate System so long 
as Silver City’s patrons retain some access. 
 Silver City responds that other PEA provisions support the district 
court’s interpretation, including Section 2.3(iv), which prohibits Siegel from 
taking actions that interfere with Silver City’s parking rights during 
construction of the parking garage. In reply, Siegel argues that Section 2.3(iv) 
does not apply until Siegel starts constructing the parking garage. 
 The district court’s July 10, 2024, order did not finally resolve the 
parties’ competing interpretations of the PEA; it determined only that Silver 
City’s interpretation was more persuasive for purposes of preliminary relief . 
Although “the scope of an easement is strictly construed in favor of the 
 4 
landowner,” City of Las Vegas v. Cliff Shadows Pro . Plaza, LLC, 129 Nev. 1, 
12, 293 P.3d 860, 867 (2013), Siegel has not shown that the district court erred 
in preliminarily determining that the PEA precludes the challenged 
obstructions. 
 Although Section 2.3(iv) expressly addresses interference during 
construction of the parking garage, that limitation does not establish that 
Siegel may obstruct access before construction begins. Additionally, Siegel’s 
argument that the PEA affords Silver City some access does not establish that 
the Fence and Gate System is consistent with the access rights granted under 
the PEA. Accordingly, Siegel has not shown that the district court committed 
reversible error in preliminarily determining that Silver City was likely to 
succeed on its claims. 
Applicability of Section 1.1(f) 
 Siegel argues that Section 1.1(f) of the PEA, which permits Silver 
City to tow unauthorized vehicles at Siegel’s expense under certain 
circumstances, applies only to vehicles parked in the parking garage, which 
has not yet been built. Accordingly, Siegel argues that the district court 
improperly relied on Section 1.1(f) in concluding that the PEA did not authorize 
the Fence and Gate System. Silver City responds that Section 1.1(f) ’s 
introductory language ties it to other rights contained in Section 1.1, including 
those that apply before construction begins. 
 Because the district court determined only that Silver City’s 
interpretation of Section 1.1 was likely correct for purposes of preliminary 
relief, we need not definitively resolve that section’s meaning. Given Section 
1.1(f)’s introductory language, we are not persuaded that the district court 
committed reversible error in preliminarily determining that Section 1.1(f) 
might apply before construction of the parking garage. Accordingly, Siegel has 
 5 
not shown error in the district court ’s evaluation of the likelihood-of-success 
factor. 
The district court’s irreparable-harm determinations are supported by 
substantial evidence 
 Siegel alternatively argues that the district court abused its 
discretion because substantial evidence does not support its finding that Silver 
City would suffer irreparable harm. See Finkel v. Cashman Pro., Inc., 128 Nev. 
68, 72-73, 270 P.3d 1259, 1262 (2012) (“A decision that lacks support in the 
form of substantial evidence is arbitrary or capricious and, therefore, an abuse 
of discretion.” (internal quotation marks omitted)). Siegel raises three 
arguments, contending that money damages would adequately compensate 
Silver City, the district court overlooked less restrictive alternatives, and the 
balance of harms favors Siegel. 
Adequacy of money damages 
Siegel argues that money damages could compensate Silver City 
for any lost revenue from the Fence and Gate System. Silver City responds 
that leaving the Fence and Gate System in place could jeopardize contractual 
relationships with Silver City’s tenants, which include Silver City’s obligations 
to provide their tenants’ customers parking access. Because such harm 
extends beyond calculable lost revenue, and Siegel does not meaningfully 
address Silver City’s contention in this respect, Siegel has not shown that the 
district court acted arbitrarily and capriciously in finding that money damages 
would be inadequate. 
Alternate ways of preventing harm 
 Siegel argues that the district court overlooked potential 
modifications to the Fence and Gate System that could have addressed Silver 
City’s access concerns without its complete removal. But Silver City’s request 
for injunctive relief was an all-or -nothing proposition, seeking removal of the 
 6 
Fence and Gate System, and Siegel identifies no specific alternative 
modifications that the district court overlooked. Accordingly, Siegel has not 
demonstrated that the district court abused its discretion in ordering the Fence 
and Gate System’s removal pending resolution of the litigation. This 
conclusion does not foreclose consideration of a modification arrangement in 
further litigation. 
Balance of harm 
Siegel contends that removal of the Fence and Gate System 
pending this litigation will expose its lot to the risks of crime and 
homelessness, thereby resulting in harm to Siegel that outweighs Silver City’s 
alleged harm from the Fence and Gate System being maintained. 
We are not persuaded that the district court committed reversible 
error solely on this issue. Namely, as the district court found, Siegel purchased 
the lot fully aware of the concerns regarding crime and homelessness 
associated with the lot. Thus, Siegel cannot rely on these perceived harms that 
existed when it purchased the lot as a justification for installing the Fence and 
Gate System thereafter. In sum, substantial evidence supports the district 
court’s findings that Silver City would likely suffer irreparable harm if the 
Fence and Gate System were to remain in place pending the litigation. 
Having considered the parties’ arguments and concluded that no 
relief is warranted, we 
 ORDER the judgment of the district court AFFIRMED. 

Bell, J. 

Stiglich, J. Cadish, J.
