-1- 
S T A T E O F M I C H I G A N 

C O U R T O F A P P E A L S 

CYNTHIA ZALEWSKI, 

 Plaintiff-Appellant, 

FOR PUBLICATION 
November 20, 2026 
11:10 AM 
v No. 378897 
Oakland Circuit Court 
US BANK TRUST NATIONAL ASSOCIATION 
TRUSTEE, as Trustee of the BKPL-EG SERIES I 
TRUST, GENISYS CREDIT UNION, DONALD 
WHITE, and HP FORECLOSURE SOLUTION, 
LLC, 

LC No. 2024-210718-CH 
 Defendants-Appellees, 

and 

SOTTILE & BARILE PLLC and CALLAHAN 
LAW PC, 

 Defendants. 

Before: ACKERMAN, P.J., and BORRELLO and KOROBKIN, JJ. 

ACKERMAN, P.J. 
 “Every mortgage of real estate, which contains a power of sale, upon default being made 
in any condition of such mortgage, may be foreclosed by advertisement, in the cases and in the 
manner specified in” chapter 32 of the Revised Judicature Act (RJA). MCL 600.3201. “ The 
statutes [governing foreclosure] were intended to prevent surprise or unfairness, and they should 
be enforced in everything substantial.” Reading v Waterman, 46 Mich 107, 110; 8 NW 691 (1881). 
These “simple and cheap remedies,” id., help make mortgage credit available to purchasers seeking 
to realize the American dream of homeownership. But the efficiency of foreclosure by 
advertisement comes with statutory safeguards, and irregularities in the foreclosure process may 
justify setting aside a sale when they prejudice a mortgagor’s ability to retain the property. 

-2- 
 This case concerns a sheriff’s deed that incorrectly identified a six -month redemption 
period when the applicable statutory period was 12 months. We conclude that this misstatement 
constituted an irregularity in the foreclosure procedure, contrary to the trial court’s determination. 
Whether that irregularity caused plaintiff Cynthia Zalewski prejudice remains for consideration on 
remand. We otherwise affirm the trial court’s rulings. 
I. BACKGROUND 
 This case involves plaintiff’s challenge to the validity of a foreclosure by advertisement on 
a home she inherited from her mother, Dorothy Zalewski. In 2007, Dorothy obtained a mortgage, 
securing $50,000 in indebtedness. By the time Dorothy passed away in January 2013 and plaintiff 
inherited the property, the mortgage had been assigned to NewRez LLC. Plaintiff then began 
making the mortgage payments, and at the time plaintiff made her last payment to NewRez, she 
owed approximately $5,800 on the underlying indebtedness. 
 Plaintiff alleges that, in 2021, she informed NewRez that her income had declined because 
of the COVID -19 pandemic and that NewRez offered to place a moratorium on the payments. 
Plaintiff did not make any further payments and alleges that she first learned of a problem with the 
loan when she discovered a notice posted on the property announcing a sheriff’s sale. By then, 
the mortgage had been assigned to defendant US Bank National Association, which acted as the 
foreclosing bank. 
 On December 12, 2023, the property was sold at the sheriff’s sale to codefendant HP 
Foreclosure Solution for approximately $180,000. The evidence of sale provided that the 
mortgagor owed $18,788.02 1 and that there was a six -month redemption period. Plaintiff soon 
recognized that because the amount owed was less than two -thirds of the original indebtedness, 
the correct redemption period was 12 months under MCL 600.3240(12). 
 After the sheriff’s sale, plaintiff spoke with a n HP representative about redeeming the 
property. During that discussion, that employee referred plaintiff to the employee ’s uncle, 
codefendant Donald White, who worked at codefendant Genisys Credit Union. Plaintiff attempted 
to inform White, Genisys, and HP that the correct redemption period was 12 months, but nothing 
changed. Just before the purported six -month redemption period expired, plaintiff set up a new 
loan with Genisys to redeem the property. Because of a three-day cooling-off period, however, 
the loan could not be processed before the six-month period expired. 
 On October 31, 2024, plaintiff filed the instant lawsuit , raising 10 relevant counts against 
numerous defendants.2 In Count I, plaintiff sought to quiet title against HP on the ground that the 

1 The apparent implication is that the $5,800 balance had increased because of interest and late 
fees. 
2 Defendants Sottile & Barile PLLC and Callahan Law PC were sued for their actions while 
representing their respective clients, US Bank and HP. Those claims were dismissed, however, 
and plaintiff does not challenge the dismissal related to th ose law firms on appeal. Plaintiff also 
does not challenge the dismissal of her counts regarding alleged violations of MCL 339.918 and 

-3- 
sheriff’s deed was defective. In Count II, plaintiff sought a declaratory judgment that US Bank 
and HP clouded title. In Count III, plaintiff alleged a claim of “inaccurate stated account,” which 
repeated her allegation that US Bank and HP clouded plaintiff’s title to the property through the 
sheriff’s deed. In Count IV, plaintiff raised a claim titled “foreclosure conducted based on 
inaccurate stated account.” The gist of that count is that because the mortgage servicers did not 
send plaintiff any statements after the moratorium was granted, the purported $18,000 amount 
owed is void. In Count V, plaintiff alleged fraudulent misrepresentation and fraud by US Bank , 
based on US Bank’s representation that she owed $18,000 instead of $5,800. In Count VI, plaintiff 
sought to void the foreclosure sale based on mistakes US Bank made leading up to the sale. In 
Count VIII, plaintiff alleged that White and Genisys breached their fiduciary duties to her by 
“slow-walking” the loan approval process, attempting to convince her that she was not entitled to 
a 12-month redemption period, and failing to inform her that she could waive her right to the three-
day cooling-off period. In Count XI, plaintiff raised a claim titled “illegal refusal of redemption 
amount” against HP. In Count XII, plaintiff alleged that HP engaged in usury by charging a per 
diem interest rate in excess of Michigan limitations . Finally, in Count XIV, plaintiff alleged 
fraudulent misrepresentation and fraud against HP. 
 On December 30, 2024, HP moved for summary disposition under MCR 2.116(C)(8) and 
(10). HP’s first argument was that, assuming plaintiff was entitled to a 12 -month redemption 
period, she lacked standing to challenge the foreclosure because she had failed to redeem the 
property within that period. The trial court agreed and granted the motion for summary disposition. 
Although the court recognized that the redemption period was 12 months, it concluded that 
plaintiff’s failure to redeem within that period deprived her of standing to challenge the foreclosure 
sale. The court acknowledged a limited exception when a party challenging the foreclosure makes 
a clear showing of fraud or irregularity in the foreclosure procedure itself but concluded that 
plaintiff had failed to establish any qualifying irregularity. 
 US Bank also moved for summary disposition under MCR 2.116(C)(8) and (10). It argued 
that plaintiff’s claims for declaratory judgment, inaccurate account stated, foreclosure based on 
inaccurate account, fraudulent misrepresentation and fraud, and voiding the foreclosure sale should 
be dismissed because she had failed to redeem the property within either the 6 - or 12 -month 
redemption period. The trial court granted the motion in its entirety. Consistent with its earlier 
ruling, the court concluded that plaintiff lacked standing to void the foreclosure sale because she 
failed to redeem the property within the applicable 12-month redemption period. 
 Genisys and White later moved for summary disposition under MCR 2.116(C)(10) on the 
remaining claim of breach of fiduciary duty against them. The trial court granted the motion, 
concluding that the evidence showed only an ordinary debtor-creditor relationship, which did not 
give rise to a fiduciary duty. 

its federal counterpart, challenging certain eviction proceedings filed against her, alleging that 
White and Genisys engaged in the unlicensed practice of law, or alleging intentional infliction of 
emotional distress. 

-4- 
II. SUMMARY DISPOSITION RULINGS 
 This Court reviews a trial court’s decision on a motion for summary disposition de novo. 
PNC Nat’l Bank Ass’n v Dep’t of Treasury, 285 Mich App 504, 505; 778 NW2d 282 (2009). The 
trial court did not specify whether it was acting under MCR 2.116(C)(8) or (10) in granting 
summary disposition. To the extent the court and the parties relied on materials outside the 
pleadings, the relief is to be considered as granted under MCR 2.116(C)(10). For claims where 
materials outside the pleadings were not relied on, MCR 2.116(C)(8) is appropriate. See Spiek v 
Dep’t of Transp, 456 Mich 331, 338; 572 NW2d 201 (1998). 
 “A motion for summary disposition brought under MCR 2.116(C)(8) tests the legal 
sufficiency of the complaint on the basis of the pleadings alone. The purpose of such a motion is 
to determine whether the plaintiff has stated a claim upon which relief can be granted.” Beaudrie 
v Henderson , 465 Mich 124, 129 -130; 631 NW2d 308 (2001). “All well -pleaded factual 
allegations are accepted as true and construed in a light most favorable to the nonmovant.” Maiden 
v Rozwood, 461 Mich 109, 119; 597 NW2d 817 (1999). “The motion should be granted if no 
factual development could possibly justify recovery.” Beaudrie, 465 Mich at 129-130. 
 A motion brought under MCR 2.116(C)(10), on the other hand, tests the factual support 
for the claim. Spiek, 456 Mich at 337. “In evaluating such a motion, a court considers the entire 
record in the light most favorable to the party opposing the motion, including affidavits, pleadings, 
depositions, admissions, and other evidence submitted by the parties.” Corley v Detroit Bd of Ed, 
470 Mich 274, 278; 681 NW2d 342 (2004). Summary disposition is appropriate when there are 
no genuine issues of material fact and the moving party is entitled to judgment as a matter of law. 
Kisiel v Holz, 272 Mich App 168, 170; 725 NW2d 67 (2006). 
A. STANDING 
 The principal issue on appeal is whether the trial court erred by granting summary 
disposition of plaintiff’s foreclosure-related claims for lack of standing. We conclude that the trial 
court erred by treating the incorrect redemption deadline in the sheriff’s deed as insufficient to 
constitute an irregularity in the foreclosure procedure. 
 The general nature of foreclosure by advertisement is well established. In the event of 
certain defaults, a lender may post a notice that the mortgage on mortgaged premises will be 
foreclosed, MCL 600.3208, after which there is to be a public sale “by the sheriff, undersheriff, or 
a deputy sheriff of the county, to the highest bidder,” MCL 600.3216. The person making the sale 
must execute “a deed of the premises bid off by him.” MCL 600.3232. 
 Even af ter the sheriff’s sale, the mortgagor retains an opportunity to reclaim the lost 
property. A sheriff’s deed “is void if the mortgagor . . . redeems the entire premises sold by paying 
the amount required . . . within the applicable time limit . . . to the purchaser . . . or to the register 
of deeds in whose office the deed is deposited.” MCL 600.3240(1). See also Bryan v JPMorgan 
Chase Bank, 304 Mich App 708, 713; 848 NW2d 482 (2014) (“Pursuant to MCL 600.3240, after 
a sheriff’s sale is completed, a mortgagor may redeem the property by paying the requisite amount 
within the prescribed time limit . . . .”). But “[i]f a mortgagor fails to avail him or herself of the 
right of redemption, all the mortgagor’s rights in and to the property are extinguished.” Id., citing 

-5- 
Piotrowski v State Land Office Bd , 302 Mich 179, 187; 4 NW2d 514 (1942). Consequently, this 
Court has held that a m

Matter of Target Corp. v County of Monroe Indus. Dev. Agency 
 2026 NY Slip Op 06899 
 November 20, 2026 
 Appellate Division, Fourth Department 
 Published by New York State Law Reporting Bureau pursuant to Judiciary Law § 431. 
 This decision is uncorrected and subject to revision before publication in the Official Reports. 

 IN THE MATTER OF TARGET CORPORATION, PETITIONER, 
 v 
 COUNTY OF MONROE INDUSTRIAL DEVELOPMENT AGENCY AND ONE MEDLEY CENTER, LLC, RESPONDENTS. 

 Supreme Court of the State of New York, Appellate Division, Fourth Judicial Department 
 Decided on November 20, 2026 
 481 OP 25-01531 
 Present: Whalen, P.J., Lindley, Ogden, Nowak, And Delconte, JJ. 

 FOGEL & BROWN P.C., SYRACUSE (MICHAEL A. FOGEL OF COUNSEL), FOR PETITIONER. 
 HARRIS BEACH MURTHA CULLINA PLLC, BUFFALO (ALLISON B. FIUT OF COUNSEL), FOR RESPONDENT COUNTY OF MONROE INDUSTRIAL DEVELOPMENT AGENCY. 

 Proceeding pursuant to EDPL 207 (initiated in the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court in the Fourth Judicial Department) to annul a determination of respondent County of Monroe Industrial Development Agency. 
[*1]
 It is hereby ORDERED that the determination is unanimously confirmed without costs and the petition is dismissed. 
 Memorandum: In this original proceeding pursuant to EDPL 207, petitioner seeks annulment of a determination of respondent County of Monroe Industrial Development Agency (COMIDA) condemning certain contractual rights of petitioner, which operates a retail store in Irondequoit, just west of the site of the shopping center once known as the Medley Centre and the Irondequoit Mall. 
 A public hearing regarding the proposed condemnation was scheduled, and COMIDA notified petitioner of the public hearing by sending a copy of the notice of public hearing and an accompanying letter by both certified mail and Federal Express to the address provided by petitioner to the tax assessor for billing purposes, as required by EDPL 202 (C) (1), within the time period set forth in EDPL 202 (C) (2). The documents informed petitioner that the hearing would address the "[p]roposed condemnation of certain real property interests held by [petitioner] . . . with respect to" certain parcels of land. The documents further informed petitioner that the purpose of the public hearing was to consider the acquisition of the property, the public purpose of the proposed acquisition, and the details of the proposed project. Despite that notice, no one appeared on petitioner's behalf at the public hearing, and the only people who spoke at the hearing expressed support for the proposed condemnation of petitioner's contractual rights. It is undisputed that the notice of public hearing did not inform petitioner that, if it wished to raise a subsequent challenge to the condemnation, it could "do so only on the basis of issues, facts, and objections raised at [the] hearing" (EDPL 202 [C] [2]). The letter that accompanied the notice did, however, contain that language in bold, underlined, and capital letters. 
 The condemnation was approved following the hearing, and COMIDA sent petitioner a synopsis of its determination and findings. Approximately one month later, petitioner commenced this proceeding contending, inter alia, that the notice of the public hearing was insufficient because it failed to inform the public and petitioner of the public use to be served by the proposed public project and describe the details of the property rights sought to be condemned and failed to state in the notice that property owners who subsequently wished to challenge condemnation via judicial review could do so only on the basis of issues, facts, and [*2] objections raised at the hearing. We reject petitioner's contention regarding the sufficiency of the notice regarding the public hearing. 
 Pursuant to the EDPL, the condemnor must provide "notice of the purpose, time, date, and location of [the] public hearing" (§ 202 [C] [1]), and we conclude that COMIDA's notice and accompanying letter to petitioner satisfied those requirements. Section 202 does not require the condemnor to describe the proposed public project sought to be undertaken. Indeed, the entire objective of the public hearing is for the condemnor to "outline the purpose . . . of the public project and any other information it considers pertinent" (EDPL 203). Notice of the purpose of the public hearing , which is required by EDPL 202, is not the same as notice of the purpose of the proposed public project , which is the objective of the public hearing and is not required to be contained in the notice of the hearing ( see EDPL 203). 
 We further conclude that the notice of public hearing and the letter accompanying the notice sent to petitioner were sufficient to inform petitioner that "property owners who may subsequently wish to challenge condemnation of their property via judicial review may do so only on the basis of issues, facts, and objections raised at such hearing," as mandated by EDPL 202 (C) (2). While the notice of public hearing did not include the statutorily required language, the statutory warning is directed only at owners of property sought to be condemned, not the public at large. Petitioner cites no authority in support of its assertion that the letter sent to petitioner, which accompanied the notice of public hearing and contained the statutory warning, should not be considered as part of the notice sent to the property owner contemplated by EDPL 202 (C) (1) and (2). 
 Petitioner raises numerous substantive contentions regarding the determination to condemn its contractual rights. We conclude that "such contentions are not properly before this Court, as . . . petitioner did not appear at the public hearing, and thus, failed to raise or present [those contentions]" ( Matter of River St. Realty Corp. v City of New Rochelle , 181 AD3d 676, 678 [2d Dept 2020]; see Matter of One Point St. , Inc. v City of Yonkers Indus. Dev. Agency , 170 AD3d 851 , 853 [2d Dept 2019]; Sun Co. v City of Syracuse Indus. Dev. Agency , 209 AD2d 34, 44 [4th Dept 1995], appeal dismissed 86 NY2d 776 [1995]). We reject petitioner's contention that EDPL 207 (A) permits it to seek judicial review of COMIDA's determination and findings even though it did not appear at the public hearing. That statute provides that "[a]ny person or persons jointly or severally, aggrieved by the condemnor's determination and findings made pursuant to [EDPL 204], may seek judicial review thereof by the appellate division of the supreme court, in the judicial department embracing the county wherein the proposed facility is located by the filing of a petition in such court within thirty days after the condemnor's completion of its publication of its determination and findings pursuant to [EDPL 204]." While EDPL 207 (A) allows petitioner, as an aggrieved party, to commence a proceeding pursuant to EDPL article 2, it does not allow petitioner to raise arguments and objections in such a proceeding that were not raised at the public hearing. 
 We thus confirm the determination and dismiss the petition. 
 Entered: November 20, 2026 
 Ann Dillon Flynn 
 Clerk of the Court

LANIER, J. 
In this matter, pro se plaintiffs/ appellants, Darrell Berry and Constance
Lafayette (" plaintiffs"), appealthe district court's July 1, 2024 judgment granting
the peremptoryexception raising the objection of res judicata filed by the
defendant/ appellee, Specialized Loan Servicing, LLC (" Specialized Loan"), and
dismissingall claims againstit, while also continuingwithout date Specialized
Loan' s other peremptory exceptions raising objections of no cause of action, 
prescription, and peremption. For the following reasons, we affirm the judgment
in part as to the exception raising the objection of resjudicata, and we amendin
part to dismiss the remaining exceptions as moot. 
FACTS AND PROCEDURAL HISTORY
This matter originated when plaintiffs borrowed a sum of money and
executed a promissory note that was secured by a mortgage encumbering their
property on December 27, 2005. Plaintiffs defaulted, and in 2017 Wells Fargo
instituted an executory process suit in the 19" Judicial District Court, Suit No. 
656991, seeking the seizure and sale of the property. The district court issued an
order authorizing executory process and a writ of seizure and sale. 
Subsequently, plaintiffs filed a separate suit in the 19th Judicial District
Court, Suit No. 672792, that was removed to the U. S. District Court for the Middle
District of Louisiana, Berry v. LoanCity, 489 F.Supp.3d 441, 444 (M.D. La. 2020) 
Berry T'). They named LoanCity; Wells Fargo; Federal Home Loan Mortgage
Corporation (" Freddie Mac"); Freddie Mac Multiclass Certificates, Series 3113
Trust, Mortgage Electronic Registration System (" MERS"); and John Does 1- 100
as defendants. Plaintiffs asserted the following causes of action: lack of
standing/wrongful foreclosure, unconscionablecontract, breach of contract, breach
of fiduciary duty, quiet title, slander of title, injunctive relief, and declaratory
relief. Plaintiffs were given an opportunity to amend their petition, and they
ON
replicated their prior petition while also adding claims that: ( 1) Wells Fargo falsely
told the district court it had riot foreclosed, and ( 2) the mortgage and note were
cancelled; thus, any assignment was null and void. The federal district court
dismissedthe claims against Wells Fargo and the Freddie Mac defendantswith
prejudice, andthe U.S. Fifth Circuit Court of Appeal affirmed Berry I' s dismissal
of the Wells Fargo and the Freddie Mac defendants. Berry v. Wells Fargo Bank, 
N. A., 20-30670521-30060, 2022WL 728969 (5th Cir. 3/10/22) (per curiam). The
U.S. Supreme Court also denied certiorari. Berry v. Wells Fargo Bank, NA., 143
S.Ct. 2585, 216 L. Ed. 2d 1194 ( 2023). 
After BerryI' s dismissalwasaffirmed, plaintiffsfiled this suit in the 19" 
Judicial District Court, Suit No. 724405 (" Berry If'), and named the following
defendants: Wells Fargo, NERS, LLC; Caliber Home Loans, Inc.; Fay Servicing, 
LLC; LSF 10 Mortgage Holdings, LLC; U.S. Bank Trust National Association as

abandonedexecutoryprocess, unfairanddeceptiveconsumerpracticesasto loan

Wells Fargo and NMRS were defendantsin Berry 1, and Specialized Loan
was added in Berry 11. SpecializedLoan was assignedthe loan by Wells Fargo in
2018accordingto thefederaldistrict court, but plaintiffs claimthis assignmentwas
false. Unlike Berry 1, however, plaintiffs now allegefactsspecificto the executory
3
proceeding, attachthe foreclosurejudgment, and seekdeclaratoryand injunctive
relief as to the foreclosure judgment. 
DefendantsremovedBerry 11to federal court, but it was remandedto the
state court where several defendants filed exceptions, and the state district court
allowed plaintiffs to file an amendedpetition that largely duplicated their original
petition in Berry 11. Plaintiffs added several claims related to the 2017 foreclosure
that challenged the various lenders/ servicers' standing under the note and
mortgage. In response, pertinent to this appeal, Specialized Loan filed peremptory
exceptions raising the objections of no cause of action, res judicata ( based on
Berry P, and prescription. 
A hearing was held on May 13, 2024, and the district court rendered the
following judgment on July 1, 2024: 
IT IS HEREBY ORDERED, ADJUDGED, AND
DECREED that the Peremptory Exception of Res Judicata filed by
Specialized Loan Servicing, LLC is GRANTED. 
IT IS FURTHER ORDERED, ADJUDGED, AND
DECREED that all claims against Specialized Loan Servicing, LLC
in the above - numbered and entitled proceeding are hereby
DISMISSED from the docket of the Court WITH PREJUDICE. 
IT IS FURTHER ORDERED, ADJUDGED, AND
DECREED that the Peremptory Exception of No Cause of Action, 
Exception of Prescription, and Exception of Peremption filed by
Specialized Loan Servicing, LLC are CONTINUED WITHOUT
DATE. 
Plaintiffs timely appealed. 
In conjunction with this appeal, plaintiffs filed the following motions: 
Motion to Stay Appellate Proceedings Pending Supervisory Review"; " Notice of
Supreme Court Mandamus Proceeding and Renewed Request for Stay of
Proceedings"; " Motion to Vacate and Strike Briefing Schedule for Lack of
Jurisdiction"; " Motion for Judicial Notice of Absence of Lodged Appellate
Record"; and " Motion to Dismiss Appeal for Lack of Appellate Jurisdiction ( Filed
0
Under Protest)." We have considered plaintiffs' motions and find they all lack
merit; thus, they aredenied. 
DISCUSSION
Procedural Issues
Plaintiffs first note their appellant brief is filed under protest to prevent
abandonment, and they do not submit to this court's jurisdiction. They maintain
that appellate jurisdiction has not attached because the appellate record in Suit No. 
656991 (the foreclosureproceeding) hasnot beenlodgedin this court. 
In sum, plaintiffs ask this court to determine appellate jurisdiction has not
attached and dismiss the appeal for lack of jurisdiction. Alternatively, they ask that
all proceedings be stayed pending resolution of the jurisdictional matter by the
Louisiana Supreme Court; or alternatively, decline to proceed until the missing
appellate record is lodged. 
Contrarily, SpecializedLoan arguesthis court hasjurisdiction, andplaintiffs
abandonedtheir claims on the merits by failing to brief them. 
Regardingthis court'sjurisdiction, thejudgmenton appealherearosein Suit
No. 724405 (plaintiffs' petition alleging defendantshad no right to foreclose), and
the record from this case has been lodged with this court. Plaintiffs maintain, 
however, that the record for Suit No. 656991 ( executory foreclosure proceeding) 
should have been lodged as well. We find that the two matters are separateand, by
plaintiffs' own admission, have never been consolidated; thus, the record on appeal
before us is complete. 
As to plaintiffs' application for a writ of mandamus before the Louisiana
Supreme Court asking that it order the 19' Judicial District Clerk to lodge the
record from Suit No. 656991 with this court, such a filing doesnot divest this court
of jurisdiction over this appeal. See Metro Riverboat Associates, Inc. v. Louisiana
Gaming Control Bd., 1999- 2241 ( La. App. 1st Cir. 3/ 7/ 01), 798 So. 2d 143, 148, 
E
writ denied, 2001- 0818 ( La. 1/ 4/ 02), 805 So. 2d 1188 ( explaining that a " writ of
mandamus is a separateand distinct remedy" from an appeal). Further, we note
the Louisiana Supreme Court denied that writ application. Berry v. Wells Fargo
Bank, NA, 2026- 00525 ( La. 9/ 16/ 26), 436 So. 3d 1263. 
As to abandonment, Specialized Loan argues the issue before us is whether
the district court properly granted its exception raising the objection of res
judicata, but plaintiffs did not address the merits; thus, they abandoned their
position. The Uniform Rules of Louisiana Courts of Appeal, Rule 2- 12.4( B)( 4), 
provides that "[ a] ll assignments of error and issues for review shall be briefed. The
courtmay deemasabandonedany assignmentof error or issuefor review which
has not been briefed." This court has found that assignments of error neither
briefed nor argued are abandoned. See State v. Gordon, 2004- 0633 ( La. App. 1st
Cir. 10/ 29/ 04), 896 So. 2d 1053, 1065, writ denied, 2004- 3144 ( La. 4/ 1/ 05), 897
So. 2d 600; Deubler v. Bogalusa City Schools, 2018- 0312 ( La. App. 1st Cir. 
9/ 21/ 18), 262 So. 3d 393, 401. Regardingpro se briefs, however, this court reads
such filings " indulgently and attemptsto construe briefs as though assignmentsof
error were properly raised." Brown v. Terrebonne Parish Sheriff' s Office, 2017- 
1305 (La. App. 1stCir. 4/13/18), 249 So. 3d 864, 869 n. 7. 
Reading plaintiffs' brief " indulgently," we find they addressedthe merits of
the resjudicata exception, although they did so tangentially. Plaintiffs spent the
bulk of their brief arguing that it was a "protective" brief filed " under protest and
does not constitute submission to the jurisdiction of this court" because appellate
jurisdiction had not attached due to the failure to lodge the record from Suit No. 
656991. Nevertheless, plaintiffs argued in the alternative that if this court ruled on
the merits, the district court should be reversed; thus, they did not abandon their
argument. 
Co
Res Judicata
As to themeritsregardingresjudicata, LouisianaRevisedStatutes13:4231
provides: 
Except as otherwise provided by law, a valid and final
judgment is conclusive between the same parties, except on appeal or
other direct review, to the following extent: 
1) If the judgment is in favor of the plaintiff, all causes of
action existing at the time of final judgment arising out of the
transaction or occurrence that is the subject matter of the litigation are
extinguished and merged in the judgment. 
2) If the judgment is in favor of the defendant, all causes of
action existing at the time of final judgment arising out of the
transaction or occurrence that is the subject matter of the litigation are
extinguished and the judgment bars a subsequent action on those
causes of action. 
3) A judgment in favor of either the plaintiff or the defendant

leads.caseName: Van Damme v. Nat'l Default Serv. Corp.
leads.text:
IN THE COURT OF APPEALS OF THE STATE OF NEVADA
ARMIN VAN DAMME,
Appellant,
vs.
NATIONAL DEFAULT SERVICING
CORPORATION,
Respondent.
No. 91398-COA
ORDER OF AFFIRMANCE
Armin Van Damme appeals from a district court order denying a
NRCP 60(b) motion to set aside a decision in a foreclosure mediation matter
and declaring him a vexatious litigant. Eighth Judicial District Court, Clark
County; Hon. Jerry A. Wiese, Judge.
In 2003, Van Damme and his then-wife Geraldine purchased a
residence in Las Vegas (the subject property). In 2004, the Van Dammes
secured a $740,000 mortgage secured by a deed of trust to refinance the subject
property. The Van Dammes subsequently defaulted on the mortgage. Since
that initial default almost two decades ago, Van Damme has initiated multiple
actions in several forums to stave off foreclosure on the subject property. In
August 2022, Van Damme recorded a grant, bargain, and sale deed conveying
ownership of the subject property to Geraldine with the Clark County
Recorder.
On April 11, 2024, respondent National Default Servicing
Corporation (NDSC) recorded a notice of default and election to sell under deed
of trust with the Clark County Recorder. That notice was subsequently served
2
on Van Damme and Geraldine on April 19, 2024, and included a written notice
regarding the Nevada Foreclosure Mediation Program. Pursuant to NRS
107.086(3), Van Damme had 30 days from the April 19, 2024, service date—i.e.,
until May 19, 2024—to petition the district court to participate in foreclosure
mediation. On July 17, 2024, NDSC filed a foreclosure mediation certificate
which stated Van Damme did not attend the foreclosure mediation conference
and that foreclosure could proceed. On December 23, 2024, NDSC recorded a
notice of trustee’s sale which indicated the subject property would be sold at
public auction in January 2025.
On December 30, 2024, Van Damme petitioned the district court
for foreclosure mediation. The next day, Van Damme filed a motion for a
temporary restraining order to halt the impending trustee sale. In the motion,
Van Damme alleged, among other things, that a notice of default recorded in
January 2008 was never rescinded and was therefore terminated under NRS
106.240, that a February 2008 loan modification he had entered into was never
funded, and that NDSC executed an improper substitution of trustee in 2013.
Van Damme also alleged that NDSC was not qualified to act as a trustee, that
the firm representing NDSC had a conflict of interest, that NDSC lacked
standing, that NDSC committed fraud, and that the beneficiary of the deed of
trust improperly expunged a lis pendens he had recorded. A week later, Van
Damme filed an “emergency motion to halt trustee sale” that was largely
reiterative of his motion for a temporary restraining order. NDSC opposed Van
Damme’s motions and counter-moved the district court to dismiss the petition.
The district court thereafter entered an amended order denying
3
Van Damme’s motions and dismissing the petition. 1 With respect to Van
Damme’s request for injunctive relief, the court concluded that such relief was
“beyond the scope of the Foreclosure Mediation Rules” and that injunctive
relief “must be sought through a separate civil action.” The court also
concluded that Van Damme did not meet the eligibility requirements of NRS
107.0865 and Foreclosure Mediation Rule 7 to participate in foreclosure
mediation because he was not an owner-occupant of the subject property
following the 2022 conveyance to Geraldine, and because his petition for
foreclosure mediation was untimely filed. In light of these conclusions, the
court dismissed Van Damme’s petition in its entirety.
Van Damme subsequently filed several motions seeking
reconsideration as well as other types of relief, including, inter alia, vacatur of
the district court’s order, declaratory and injunctive relief, sanctions against
NDSC’s counsel, referral to federal enforcement agencies, and a halt of the
impending auction of the subject property. These motions were largely
repetitive of each other and included multiple exhibits Van Damme included
with his initial filings.
The district court subsequently held a hearing on Van Damme’s
motions. At that hearing, counsel for NDSC notified the district court that the
subject property had sold. The court later entered a written order denying Van
Damme’s motions, in which it concluded that Van Damme had failed to
demonstrate the court had made a clerical mistake, or a mistake arising from
1The original order entered by the district court erroneously included
language ordering the issuance of a certificate of foreclosure; the amended
order removed that language and left the remainder of the order intact.
4
oversight or omission which warranted reconsideration. The court also noted
that, as in his prior filings, Van Damme requested relief beyond what the court
could grant in a foreclosure mediation, and that in any event, “the relief sought
by [ ] Van Damme is [m]oot because a foreclosure sale has seemingly already
happened outside of the Foreclosure Mediation Program.”
Van Damme continued to file motions with the district court,
including motions seeking forms of relief that the court had previously
concluded were outside the scope of relief available in foreclosure mediation.
The court entered an order denying all these motions. The court noted that
Van Damme had raised “no new substantive arguments” since it had ruled on
his first motion for reconsideration, and warned Van Damme that should he
“continue to file [r]equests based on the same allegations previously ruled on,
this Court may issue a show cause order” requiring him “to explain why these
filings are not being filed to delay hearings, or harass the judge, and explain
why he should not be deemed a vexatious litigant.” The court also noted that
Van Damme continued to request unavailable relief, and that Van Damme was
not eligible to participate in the foreclosure mediation program.
Van Damme subsequently filed motions seeking reconsideration or
clarification of the district court’s order and information concerning the deed
of trust. Van Damme included multiple exhibits he had previously submitted
to the district court and requested the same forms of relief the court had
already declined to grant.
The district court thereafter entered an order denying those
motions. The court reiterated its prior findings that Van Damme was not
eligible to participate in the foreclosure mediation program. The court also
found that Van Damme had not raised any new substantive arguments or
5
produced any new evidence, and that there was “no additional relief” it could
grant to Van Damme. Further, the court warned Van Damme for the second
time that should he continue to request unavailable relief or continue to file
requests based on the same allegations previously ruled on, the court would
issue an order to show cause requiring Van Damme to “explain why these
filings are not being filed to delay hearings, or harass the court and opposing
counsel, and explain why he should not be deemed a vexatious litigant, and
subject to sanctions.”
One day after the district court denied Van Damme’s motion for
reconsideration and motion to compel, Van Damme filed another motion for
reconsideration in which he alleged that, among other things, the court
violated his rights to due process by denying the motion to compel without
conducting a hearing. Subsequently, Van Damme filed a supplemental motion
seeking to present new evidence and seeking reconsideration. Van Damme
presented many of the same arguments and exhibits he had presented in his
prior filings, and requested forms of relief the court had previously deemed
unavailable.
The district court subsequently entered an order denying this
latest motion and supplement. As it had in its prior orders, the court noted it
had already determined that Van Damme was not eligible to participate in the
foreclosure mediation program, and that Van Damme had not presented any
new substantive arguments or new evidence. The court concluded that it had
“now ruled on [ ] Van Damme’s Motions to Reconsider three times” and there
was “no additional relief” it could grant him. The following day, Van Damme
filed a motion seeking, among other things, relief under NRCP 60(b), which
6
reiterated several arguments he had presented in his earlier filings. Van
Damme later filed a supplement to that motion.
The district court thereafter issued an order to show cause why
Van Damme should not be declared a vexatious litigant and set a hearing
concerning that issue. The order notified Van Damme that the hearing would
consider the four factors set forth in Jordan v. State ex rel. Dept. of Motor
Vehicles, 121 Nev. 44, 110 P.3d 30 (2005), and observed that Van Damme
appeared to have “filed numerous rogue, fugitive, or unmeritorious documents”
in the case, that the filings “share similar attributes, as despite prior warnings
from this court, each request, including the three motions to reconsider, seems
to request relief this [c]ourt cannot grant,” and that the filings “appear to be
for an improper purpose, such as to harass, vex, annoy, or increase [the] cost
of litigation, but fail to assert meritorious grounds for relief.” The order also
warned Van Damme of the potential restrictions the court could impose on him
should it deem him a vexatious litigant. The district court also entered an
order denying Van Damme’s recent filings.
Van Damme later filed a motion to vacate the district court’s
orders. Two days later, Van Damme filed an opposition to the court’s order to
show cause. In his opposition, Van Damme argued that his filings were not
vexatious because they were “responsive to [NDSC’s] fraudulent actions,” and
that the district court did not have subject matter jurisdiction over him as a
“non-party” given that he had conveyed the subject property to Geraldine.
The district court held a hearing on the order to show cause. The
court opened the hearing by identifying each pleading and paper Van Damme
had filed in the case, noting that although a select few of Van Damme’s filings
were nonfrivolous, the rest were “one motion after another seeking the same
7
relief or arguing that [the court does not] have authority to do what [it] did,”
despite being told that he could seek relief via an appeal to the appellate courts.
When presented with the opportunity at the hearing to address whether his
filings were frivolous or harassing, Van Damme instead reiterated his
underlying claims.
The district court subsequently entered a written order declaring
Van Damme a vexatious litigant. The order identified 19 different filings Van
Damme made in the case and concluded that an overwhelming majority of the
filings were made without an objective good faith expectation of prevailing, and
that several of those bad-faith filings “needlessly caused expense to the other
side.” The court then made substantive findings regarding the frivolous or
harassing nature of Van Damme’s actions. The court noted that Van Damme
had filed “numerous lawsuits” relating to the subject property. The court also
found that the “entire case record demonstrated repetitive and harassing
activities” and that Van Damme’s filings lacked “an arguable factual or legal
basis.” The court further found that Van Damme filed his motions with the
intent to harass. The court also found that Van Damme’s repetitive filings
caused NDSC to retain counsel and incur legal fees. To curb further vexatious
filings, the court ordered that Van Damme (1) could not submit any additional
motions or documents in the case without prior approval of the presiding judge;
and (2) could not initiate any new “foreclosure mediation cases” related to the
subject property without prior review and approval of the chief judge of the
district. The court added that its order did not preclude Van Damme from
“opening a new District Court case seeking relief appropria

leads.caseName: 320 Alemany LLC v. City & County of San Francisco CA1/5
leads.text:
1 
Filed 11/20/26 320 Alemany LLC v. City & County of San Francisco CA1/5 
NOT TO BE PUBLISHED IN OFFICIAL REPORTS 

California Rules of Court, rule 8.1115(a), prohibits courts and parties from citing or relying on opinions not certified for 
publication or ordered published, except as specified by rule 8.1115(b). This opinion has not been certified for publication or 
ordered published for purposes of rule 8.1115. 

IN THE COURT OF APPEAL OF THE STATE OF CALIFORNIA 

FIRST APPELLATE DISTRICT 

DIVISION FIVE 

320 ALEMANY LLC, 
 Plaintiff and Appellant, 
v. 
CITY AND COUNTY OF SAN 
FRANCISCO, 
 Defendant and Respondent. 

 A173613 

 (City & County of San Francisco 
 Super. Ct. No. CPF-24-518821) 

 Plaintiff 320 Alemany LLC appeals from a judgment entered in favor of 
the City and County of San Francisco (City) on its petition for writ of 
administrative mandamus challenging the City’s determination that the 
density bonus law (Gov. Code, § 65915)1 does not apply to plaintiff’s proposed 
project. At issue is whether the density bonus law applies when a developer 
builds excess unauthorized dwelling units without permits and then later 
seeks to legalize the additional units. We find the density bonus law does not 
apply under the circumstances of this case. 

1 All statutory references are to the Government Code unless otherwise 
stated. 

 2 
FACTUAL AND PROCEDURAL BACKGROUND 
 Plaintiff owns four lots at 316–328 Alemany Boulevard. In 2002–2003, 
plaintiff subdivided a single parcel into four separate lots. Between 2004 and 
2006, plaintiff obtained four building permits to construct four separate 
residential buildings, one on each lot. The permits authorized plaintiff to 
construct a total of 15 dwelling units across the four lots as follows: five 
dwelling units on 316–318 Alemany Boulevard, three dwelling units on 320 
Alemany Boulevard, three dwelling units on 322 Alemany Boulevard, and 
four dwelling units on 326–328 Alemany Boulevard. Plaintiff does not claim 
that prior to construction it sought approval to build additional units under 
the density bonus law. Plaintiff completed construction of the 15 permitted 
units in 2008. Shortly thereafter, plaintiff divided the 15 units to add 17 
additional, unpermitted dwelling units (UDU) across the properties, resulting 
in the following total numbers of dwelling units: five permitted units and 
seven UDU’s on 316–318 Alemany Boulevard, three permitted units and 
three UDU’s on 320 Alemany Boulevard, three permitted units and four 
UDU’s on 322 Alemany Boulevard, and four permitted units and three UDU’s 
on 326–328 Alemany Boulevard. 
 In 2022, the City’s planning department (department), pursuant to a 
task force inspection of the properties, determined that the permitted units 
had been partitioned to create the additional 17 UDU’s. The City’s various 
departments issued multiple notices of violation related to safety issues at 
the properties, including inadequate fire escapes. 
 On May 30, 2023, the City filed an enforcement action against plaintiff, 
alleging violations of various state and local codes. On April 15, 2024, the 
parties stipulated to an injunction and order requiring plaintiff to bring the 
properties into compliance with state and local codes, and to the extent the 

 3 
abatement of certain violations required permits, plaintiff was required to 
take all steps necessary to obtain the permits. The stipulated judgment also 
required plaintiff to pay administrative penalties, attorneys fees, and costs 
totaling approximately $1.5 million. The injunction also prohibits plaintiff 
from accepting new tenants at the properties until all notices of violation are 
abated and the City’s department of building inspection issues a final 
certificate of completion. 
 Plaintiff communicated with the department regarding plaintiff’s 
proposals for legalizing the UDU’s. On March 18, 2024, in response to the 
department’s plan check letter No. 2, plaintiff’s architect submitted a 
proposal to maximize the number of allowable legalized units using the state 
density bonus law.2 (§ 65915.) According to plaintiff’s architect, the proposal 
would allow for 31 residential units across the properties following 
legalization. On April 24, 2024, the department responded that plaintiff’s 
proposal was not eligible under the density bonus law because the proposal 
did not result in an increase of five base units.3 
 Plaintiff requested a letter of determination from the zoning 
administrator regarding the application of the density bonus law (§ 65915) to 
the properties. The zoning administrator’s August 23, 2024, letter of 
determination confirmed that the density bonus law did not apply to 
plaintiff’s proposed project. It did not qualify as a housing development 
under the statute. Plaintiff appealed the zoning administrator’s 

2 Neither party provides a record citation to the March 18, 2024 letter 
containing the proposal and it does not appear to be in the appellate record. 
However, the letter is referenced in a declaration from plaintiff’s architect 
and in subsequent correspondence from the City. 
3 The department’s correspondence states that base units means 
principally permitted units. 

 4 
determination to the San Francisco Board of Appeals, which unanimously 
found that the zoning administrator did not err or abuse his discretion in 
issuing the letter of determination. 
 Plaintiff filed a petition for writ of administrative mandamus in the 
trial court challenging the City’s determination that the density bonus law 
did not apply to plaintiff’s project. The trial court denied the petition, finding 
the City correctly interpreted section 65915. It explained that plaintiff’s 
“project is not eligible under the statute because the legalization of unlawful 
dwelling units does not constitute a ‘housing development.’ The statute’s 
plain text supports [the City’s] argument that a ‘housing development’ 
requires construction of new units. For instance, Section 65915(b)(1) makes 
clear that an applicant must ‘construct a housing development’ to receive the 
Density Bonus Law’s benefits. Petitioner has also not shown that the units 
are subdivisions or common interest developments as defined by Civil Code 
Section 4100, nor that there would be a net increase in available units. 
Petitioner also cites no cases where plans to legalize units were eligible under 
the statute.” 
DISCUSSION 
I. Issues and Standard of Review 
 Plaintiff argues that (1) the density bonus law preempts local 
regulations and (2) the City and the trial court erroneously interpreted the 
density bonus law when they determined plaintiff’s project to legalize its 
UDU’s is not a housing development under the statute. Plaintiff’s petition for 
writ of administrative mandamus alleged the letter of determination was 
legally erroneous in concluding that the density bonus law did not apply to 

 5 
plaintiff’s project and thus was an abuse of discretion.4 “Abuse of discretion 
is established if the [agency] has not proceeded in the manner required by 
law, the order or decision is not supported by the findings, or the findings are 
not supported by the evidence.” (Code Civ. Proc., § 1094.5, subd. (b).) On 
appeal, our role is the same as the trial court. We “ ‘independently 
determine[] whether the agency prejudicially abused its discretion by failing 
to proceed in the manner required by law, such as by failing to comply with 
required procedures, applying an incorrect legal standard, or committing 
some other error of law.’ ” (Schreiber v. City of Los Angeles (2021) 69 
Cal.App.5th 549, 554.) 
 “The fundamental rule of statutory construction is to ascertain the 
Legislature’s intent in order to give effect to the purpose of the law. 
[Citation.] We first examine the words of the statute and try to give effect to 
the usual, ordinary import of the language while not rendering any language 
surplusage. The words must be construed in context and in light of the 
statute’s obvious nature and purpose. The terms of the statute must be given 
a reasonable and commonsense interpretation that is consistent with the 
Legislature’s apparent purpose and intention. [Citation.] Our interpretation 
should be practical, not technical, and should also result in wise policy, not 
mischief or absurdity. [Citation.] We do not interpret statutes in isolation. 
Instead, we read every statute with reference to the entire scheme of law of 
which it is a part in order to harmonize the whole. [Citation.]” (Kalnel 

4 The petition also alleged the City exceeded its jurisdiction and/or 
violated its ministerial duty in issuing the letter of determination and/or the 
letter of determination is not supported by the findings and the findings are 
not supported by the evidence. However, on appeal, plaintiff argues only 
legal error. 

 6 
Gardens, LLC v. City of Los Angeles (2016) 3 Cal.App.5th 927, 938 (Kalnel 
Gardens).) 
 If there is no ambiguity in the statutory language, the plain meaning of 
the statute governs. (Reznitskiy v. County of Marin (2022) 79 Cal.App.5th 
1016, 1025.) If the statutory language is ambiguous or susceptible of more 
than one reasonable interpretation, we may also look to extrinsic aids, 
including legislative history and public policy. (Id. at p. 1025.) 
II. The Density Bonus Law 
 “In 1979, the Legislature enacted the density bonus law, section 65915, 
which aims to address the shortage of affordable housing in California. 
[Citation.] ‘Although application of the statute can be complicated, its aim is 
fairly simple: When a developer agrees to construct a certain percentage of 
the units in a housing development for low- or very-low-income households, 
. . . the city or county must grant the developer one or more itemized 
concessions and a “density bonus,” which allows the developer to increase the 
density of the development by a certain percentage above the maximum 
allowable limit under local zoning law. [Citation.] In other words, the 
Density Bonus Law, “reward[s] a developer who agrees to build a certain 
percentage of low-income housing with the opportunity to build more 
residences than would otherwise be permitted by the applicable local 
regulations.” ’ [Citation.]” (Latinos Unidos Del Valle De Napa Y Solano v. 
County of Napa (2013) 217 Cal.App.4th 1160, 1164, 1st & 4th bracketed 
insertions added (Latinos Unidos).) 
 Section 65915, subdivision (b)(1) requires a city, county, or city and 
county to grant a density bonus “if an applicant for a housing development 
seeks and agrees to construct a housing development, excluding any units 
permitted by the density bonus awarded pursuant to this section,” that will 

 7 
contain at least a certain percentage of units for lower income households or 
other qualifying groups such as senior citizens, transitional foster youth, or 
students. (§ 65915, subd. (b)(1), italics added.) At issue in this appeal is the 
question of whether plaintiff’s proposal to legalize multiple existing UDU’s 
qualifies as a housing development that is eligible for a density bonus under 
the statute. 
 Section 65915, subdivision (i) states: “ ‘Housing development,’ as used 
in this section, means a development project for five or more residential 
units, including mixed-use developments. For the purposes of this section, 
‘housing development’ also includes a subdivision or common interest 
development, as defined in Section 4100 of the Civil Code,[5] approved by a 
city, county, or city and county and consists of residential units or 
unimproved residential lots and either a project to substantially rehabilitate 
and convert an existing commercial building to residential use or the 
substantial rehabilitation of an existing multifamily dwelling, as defined in 
subdivision (d) of Section 65863.4,[6] where the result of the rehabilitation 
would be a net increase in available residential units.” 
III. Density Bonus

leads.caseName: Spencer v. City of Henderson
leads.text:
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF THE STATE OF NEVADA
SONG SPENCER, AN INDIVIDUAL;
AND JAMES SPENCER, AN
INDIVIDUAL,
Appellants,
vs.
CITY OF HENDERSON, A MUNICIPAL
CORPORATION AND A POLITICAL
SUBDIVISION OF THE STATE OF
NEVADA,
Respondent.
No. 88629
SONG SPENCER,
Appellant,
vs.
CITY OF HENDERSON, A MUNICIPAL
CORPORATION AND A POLITICAL
SUBDIVISION OF THE STATE OF
NEVADA,
Respondent.
No. 89007
ORDER OF AFFIRMANCE
These are consolidated appeals from a district court dismissal
order and a post-judgment order denying attorney fees in a civil forfeiture
proceeding. Eighth Judicial District Court, Clark County; Nadia Krall,
Judge.
Respondent City of Henderson filed a civil forfeiture complaint
against $21,563 seized from appellants James and Song Spencer’s home
pursuant to a search warrant. In that complaint, the City named and
served James as a claimant. James and Song filed answers and asserted
counterclaims against the City, alleging the seized money lawfully belonged
to Song and contesting the constitutionality of Nevada’s civil forfeiture
2
scheme. About a month later, the City returned the money plus interest to
Song, and the district court thereafter dismissed the civil forfeiture
complaint as moot. It also dismissed the Spencers’ counterclaims after
concluding counterclaims are not cognizable in an in rem forfeiture action.
Song moved for attorney fees as sanctions under NRS 18.010 and
NRS 7.085, and the district court denied that motion.1
The district court properly dismissed the Spencers’ counterclaims
On appeal, the Spencers first argue that counterclaims are
permitted in Nevada civil forfeiture actions and that the district court erred
in dismissing them. We review this statutory interpretation question de
novo. See Slade v. Caesars Ent. Corp. , 132 Nev. 374, 376, 373 P.3d 74, 75
(2016).
Nevada’s civil forfeiture scheme is found in NRS 179.1156–.121.
NRS 179.1156. Civil forfeiture falls within NRS Chapter 179, “Special
Proceedings of a Criminal Nature,” despite being a civil action. See State v.
Clark, 114 Nev. 319, 321, 956 P.2d 83, 84 (1998) (noting forfeiture
proceedings against a vehicle were civil in rem proceedings). Special
proceedings are governed by the statutes that create them and are strictly
limited to the procedures those statutes provide. See, e.g. , Preferred
Equities Corp. v. State Eng’r , 119 Nev. 384, 388, 75 P.3d 380, 383 (2003)
(explaining water law proceedings “are special in character” and “strictly
1We note Song did not properly move to intervene. See NRCP 24;
Aetna Life & Cas. Ins. Co. v. Rowan , 107 Nev. 362, 363, 812 P.2d 350, 350
(1991) (“[A] proposed intervenor does not become a party to a lawsuit unless
and until the district court grants a motion to intervene.”). However, the
City did not protest Song’s participation below, and the district court treated
her as a participant, so we treat the issue as waived. Cf. Pelletier v. Pelletier,
103 Nev. 408, 410-11, 742 P.2d 1027, 1028 (1987) (addressing the merits
where the nonparty proceeded in the case below with the “apparent consent
of the parties”)
3
limit[ed]” to the method of procedure provided by statute (internal
quotations omitted)); 1A C.J.S. Actions § 283 (addressing special
proceedings); see also Leigh-Pink v. Rio Props., LLC, 138 Nev. 530, 536, 512
P.3d 322, 327 (2022) (explaining a statute’s plain language controls).
Though NRS 179.1171(1) incorporates the Nevada Rules of Civil Procedure
as the rules of practice in a forfeiture action, those “rules do not govern
procedure and practice in any special statutory proceeding insofar as they
are inconsistent or in conflict with the procedure and practice provided by
the applicable statutes.” NRCP 81(a); see NRS 179.1171(1) (stating that the
NRCP apply “except as otherwise provided in NRS 179.1156 to 179.1205,
inclusive).
The civil forfeiture statutes establish a special statutory
proceeding that, by its terms, is purely in rem. See United States v. Obaid,
971 F.3d 1095, 1099 (9th Cir. 2020) (recognizing civil forfeitures are in rem
proceedings). NRS 179.1171(4) expressly declares: “A proceeding for
forfeiture is in rem.” Consistent therewith, both NRS 179.1171(3)(a) and
NRS 179.1171(4) require the seizing agency to file its forfeiture complaint
in the district court in the county where the property is located. And,
collectively, the forfeiture statutes demonstrate civil forfeiture proceedings
are narrowly anchored to the disposition of the res. See, e.g., Chapman v.
Deutsche Bank Nat’l Tr. Co., 129 Nev. 314, 318, 302 P.3d 1103, 1106 (2013)
(explaining an in rem proceeding “is one taken directly against the property,
and has for its object the disposition of the property” (internal quotations
omitted)). For example, NRS 179.1164 and NRS 179.1165 describe the
property subject to forfeiture and address its seizure. NRS 179.1173
governs court proceedings for the property’s forfeiture, and NRS 179.1175
and NRS 179.118 regulate the disposition and distribution of property
declared forfeited. Civil forfeitures take priority over other civil actions and
4
require the property’s return within seven business days if a court
determines it is not subject to forfeiture. NRS 179.1173(1), (8).
The only parties to a forfeiture proceeding are “the plaintiff”
and “any claimant”—defendants and counterclaimants are not
contemplated. NRS 179.1171(7). The statutes give claimants the right to
answer the complaint and serve objections to written interrogatories, but
say nothing of other actions. NRS 179.1171(6). Significantly, nothing in the
statutes contemplates action or relief in the civil forfeiture itself beyond the
disposition of the res. See, e.g., Obaid, 971 F.3d at 1098 (explaining in rem
jurisdiction). And though NRS 179.1171 provides that a forfeiture
complaint should be treated as a counterclaim to a first-filed claim for
delivery action, it does not contemplate the converse—the filing of
counterclaims for damages or affirmative relief requiring in personam
jurisdiction in a first-filed forfeiture action. NRS 179.1171(2). Instead,
consistent with the pure in rem nature of the action, the only relief afforded
a successful claimant is the return of the property plus interest. NRS
179.1173(8). Cf. UMLIC VP LLC v. Matthias , 364 F.3d 125, 134 (3d Cir.
2004) (addressing mortgage foreclosure actions and explaining that “money
damages are not acquired through in rem proceedings”).
Here, the City’s civil forfeiture action against the $21,563
became moot when the City returned that money plus interest to Song. See
Valdez-Jimenez v. Eighth Jud. Dist. Ct. , 136 Nev. 155, 158, 460 P.3d 976,
981 (2020) (explaining an action is moot once there is no longer a live
controversy that a judgment can redress). The Spencers nevertheless
sought to pursue special and punitive damages through their constitutional
and tort counterclaims based on alleged violations that, if resolved, would
require the district court to move beyond its statutory authority to
adjudicate the rights to the property to the vindication of personal rights.
5
See NRS 179.1171(4). Even Song’s claim for delivery counterclaim2 is not a
pure in rem claim but rather a mixed action in which she seeks special
damages of attorney fees. See Fredericks v. Tracy, 33 P. 750, 751 (Cal. 1893)
(describing a claim and delivery action as a mixed action: in rem as to the
wrongfully taken property, and in personam as to the damages); Preston A.
Blair Co. v. Rose, 51 P.2d 209, 211 (Idaho 1935) (same); 77 C.J.S. Replevin §
5 (same). As such, it too sought relief beyond that which the civil forfeiture
statutes permit.
The district court therefore did not err by dismissing the
counterclaims, nor by dismissing the civil forfeiture action as moot. In view
of the foregoing, we need not reach the Spencers’ additional arguments
regarding Song’s entitlement to seek special damages of attorney fees on her
claim for delivery counterclaim or the constitutionality of Nevada’s
forfeiture scheme. Nor need we reach the Spencers’ argument in their reply
brief regarding mootness exceptions. See, e.g., Khoury v. Seastrand , 132
Nev. 520, 530 n.2, 377 P.3d 81, 88 n.2 (2016) (noting we need not address
appellate arguments asserted for the first time on reply). We note, however,
that nothing in this order bars claimants from pursuing their tort and
constitutional claims in a separate action.3
The district court properly denied Song’s request for attorney fees
2While we do not resolve this issue, we also note that this
counterclaim may be statutorily barred, as the City brought its forfeiture
complaint within 60 days. See NRS 179.1171(2) (explaining the property is
subject to a claim for delivery action “only if” the government does not file
the forfeiture complaint within 60 days); NRS 31.840 (allowing a claim for
delivery “[e]xcept as provided in NRS 179.1171”).
 3The parties represented at oral argument that a separate action has
been filed but stayed pending resolution of this appeal.
6
Song also challenges the denial of her request for attorney fees
as statutory sanctions under NRS 18.010(2)(b) and NRS 7.085. The district
court’s decision is reviewed for an abuse of discretion. Stubbs v. Strickland,
129 Nev. 146, 152, 297 P.3d 326, 330 (2013). NRS 18.010(2)(b) allows the
district court to award attorney fees to a prevailing party where the
complaint “was brought or maintained without reasonable ground or to
harass the prevailing party.” Similarly, NRS 7.085 permits an attorney fees
award against counsel who either files or maintains an action that is “not
well-grounded in fact[,] not warranted by existing law,” or who
“[u]nreasonably and vexatiously” extends that litigation in court. The
purpose of these statutes is to punish and deter claims that “overburden
limited juridical resources, hinder the timely resolution of meritorious
claims and increase the costs of engaging in business and providing
professional services to the public.” NRS 7.085(2); NRS 18.010(2)(b). These
sanctions “target[ ] only how the litigation itself is conducted, not what the
parties did before the litigation commenced.” In re Execution of Search
Warrants for: 12067 Oakland Hills, Las Vegas, Nev. 89141 , 134 Nev. 799,
803, 435 P.3d 672, 676 (Ct. App. 2018) (addressing NRS 18.010(2)(b)).
Further, a claim is only frivolous or groundless if there is no credible
evidence to support it. Capanna v. Orth, 134 Nev. 888, 895, 432 P.3d 726,
734 (2018).
The district court found, among other things, that the forfeiture
action was grounded in fact and warranted under existing law, that the City
reasonably relied on the result of the police investigation conducted
pursuant to a search warrant issued upon a finding of probable cause, that
Song was not prejudiced by the City’s failure to name her as a claimant or
serve her personally, and that the City’s post-filing actions were not
frivolous. The record supports the district court’s findings and weighs
7
against the Spencers’ arguments. Further, many of the Spencers’
arguments go to the Henderson Police Department’s pre-litigation conduct
rather than the City’s litigation decisions. Some arguments—such as that
the City threatened criminal contempt—are simply belied by the record.
And though the Spencers speculate about the officers’ motives and
knowledge, and fault the City for not naming Song as a claimant initially,
the record does not support that the City’s decision to file a forfeiture
complaint against the seized cash was not based on credible evidence at the
time, or that the forfeiture complaint was unreasonably or vexatiously
maintained during the three months it was pending.
Accordingly, we
ORDER the judgments of the district court AFFIRMED.
Herndon, C.J.
Pickering, J. Parraguirre, J.
Bell, J. Stiglich, J.
Cadish, J. Lee, J.

FIELDS, J. 
Defendant -appellant, Arch Insurance Company (" Arch"), appeals the trial
court' sjudgment denying its " Motion to StayandEnjoinEnforcementof Writs of
Fieri Facias, GarnishmentOrders, andNotices of Seizureandto Set for Immediate
Hearing" (" motion for preliminary injunction"). After the appeal was lodged, 
plaintiff - appellee, Jacob Tramble, as curator for Sherri Tramble (" Tramble"), filed
a motion to dismiss the appeal. For the following reasons, we grant the motion to
dismiss the appeal and dismiss the appeal as moot. 
FACTS AND PROCEDURAL HISTORY
Followingamotorvehicleaccident, TramblesuedJoshuaBriscoe, thedriver
of the other vehicle, Briscoe' s employer, Linetec Service, L.L.C. (" Linetec"), and
its insurer, Arch, in theTwenty -SeventhJudicialDistrictCourtfor theParishof St. 
Landry. Tramblev. Briscoe, 2025-423 (La. App. 3Cir. 7/2/26),2026 WL 19051411
1-2, writs denied, 2026- 00996 and 2026- 01043 ( La 10/ 28/ 26), _ So. 3d—, 2026
WL 3228208. After the trial of the matter, on November 14, 2024, the trial court
signed a $ 219, 742,924. 31 plus interest and costs second amended judgment (" the
money judgment") in favor of Tramble and against Briscoe, Linetec, and Arch. See
Id. at *2. Briscoe and Linetec appealed, and the Third Circuit amended the judgment
award to $ 40, 000, 000. 00 in general damages and $ 41, 300, 219. 00 in future medical
expenses and affirmed the judgment as amended. Id. at * 28. Arch was not an
appellant in that appeal. 
While the matter was pending on appeal, on November 21, 2025, Tramble
filed an exparte petition to makethe moneyjudgmentexecutoryin theNineteenth
Judicial District Court for the Parish of East Baton Rouge. In the petition, Tramble
allegedthatheobtainedamoneyjudgmentagainstArchonNovember14, 2024, for
219, 742, 924. 31. Tramble further alleged that since the judgment was rendered, 
Arch hadnot taken a suspensiveappealandthe delaytherefore hadexpired. Tramble
3
assertedthatthemoneyjudgmenthadnotbeenfully paidby Arch, andtherefore, 
Tramblewishedto make the judgment executoryin East Baton RougeParish. 
Tramblerequestedthatthecourtmakethejudgmentexecutoryon anexparte basis
asauthorizedby La. CodeCiv. P. art. 2782. 
On November 25, 2025, the trial court signed ajudgment, making the money
judgmentexecutory. TramblesubsequentlyfilednumerousSupplementalPetitions
for Garnishmentof AccountsandRequestsfor Writs of Fieri Faciasagainstdozens
of Arch' s business partners— including banks, brokers, and third - party
administrators— purportedlyin possessionof Arch'sproperty. Thetrial courtsigned
multiple orders, orderingthe seizureof Arch' sassets. 
On December 7, 2025, Arch filed its motion for preliminary injunction and
memorandum in support thereof. Therein, Arch contended the trial court violated
the Louisianaand U.S. constitutionsby ordering seizureof its assetsto executea
personalinjuryjudgmentbecauseit wasadirectactiondefendantthatpaidits full
policylimit. Archfurthercontendedthatasadirectactiondefendant, it couldhave
no liability beyondits policy limits.' Arch notedthat the moneyjudgment had been
suspensivelyappealedby BriscoeandLinetec. Therefore, Arch arguedthemoney
judgment was not a final, enforceablejudgment. Finally, Arch arguedthat the many
procedural defects in the action violated its due process rights. Arch also requested
attorneys' fees under La. Code Civ. P. art. 2298. 
In support of its motion for preliminary injunction, Arch attached the
following exhibits: Tramble'sJune8, 2022petitionfor damages; Arch's Insurance
BusinessAuto Declarationfor policy no. ZACAT9262801; theNovember14, 2024
moneyjudgment; theJune27, 2025PartialSatisfactionof Judgment; thetranscript
I Arch allegedthat the terms and limits of Arch' s Policy were producedin discovery andadmitted
into evidence without objection at the trial of the underlying matter. 
M
of October31, 2024hearingonArch' smotion for newtrial; andtheDecember18, 
2024ordergrantingBriscoeandLinetec'sjoint motion for suspensiveappeal. 
Tramble opposed Arch' s motion for preliminary injunction. Tramble
contended that Arch could not collaterally attack the money judgment. Tramble
furthercontendedthatthemoneyjudgmentwasa finaljudgmentagainstArch from
which no appeal lies; therefore, no court had jurisdiction to change the money
judgment " regardless of the magnitude of thefinal judgment' s error." ( Emphasis in
original). Tramble also argued that Arch did not benefit from the appeals filed by
Briscoe and Linetec. Tramble pointed out that Arch' s proposed order that requested
that Tramble be enjoined without a hearing was a TRO and arguedthe garnishments
are procedurally proper under the Louisiana Code of Civil Procedure. Finally, 
Tramble contendedthat Arch' srequestedrelief required a contradictory hearing and
a stay had no basisin law. 
FollowinganemergencyhearingonDecember17, 2025, thetrial courtdenied
Arch'smotionforpreliminaryinjunction.2Thetrial courtalsodeniedArch'srequest
to staythe effect of the denialof its motion for preliminary injunction while Arch
sought relief with this court. The trial court also excluded the affidavit of Brian First, 
President of Arch, which Arch filed in support of its motion for preliminary
injunction, but allowed Arch to proffer the affidavit. A judgment to that effect was
signedon January6, 2026. Arch appealsthe trial court's denial of its motion for
preliminary injunction.' 
zOn December19, 2025, this courtissuedan interim orderstayingthe trial court's December17, 
2025 ruling, which denied Arch' s Motion to Stay and Enjoin Enforcementof Writs of Fieri Facias, 
Garnishment Orders and Notices of Seizure and the Execution of all Writs of Fieri Facias, Garnishment
OrdersandNotices of Seizure. Tramble v. Briscoe, 2025-1310 (La. App. 1stCir. 12/19/25) (unpublished). 
On February23, 2026, this court lifted thestay. Tramble v. Briscoe, 2025-1310 (La. App. 1stCir. 2/23/26), 
2026 WL 497535, * 1, writ denied, 2026- 00250 ( La. 4/ 28/ 26), 432 So. 3d 121 ( per curiam). The supreme
court stayedthe matter but subsequentlylifted the stay. Tramble v. Briscoe, 2026-00250 (La. 4/28/26), 
432 So. 3d 121 ( per curiam). 
3 On December 18, 2025, Arch filed a motion to appeal the trial court' s December 17, 2025 order
issuedin open court denying Arch' s "Motion to Stay and Enjoin Enforcementof Writ of Fieri Facias, 
GarnishmentOrders, andNotices of Seizureand its requestof preliminary injunction therein", and the trial
court granted Arch' s motion to appeal on December 22, 2025. The judgment was signed on January 6, 
R
ASSIGNMENTS OF ERROR
1. The [ trial court] disregarded the Judgment language casting Arch in
judgment only " as insurer of the employer, Linetec," and authorized
executionbeyondArch's Policy limit in contraventionof Louisiana
Supreme Court precedent— interpretingevenmore generaljudgment
language— which held that, absent proof of bad faith, an insurer cannot
be held liable beyond its policy limit.... 
2. The [trial court] ignored the Judgment's languageexplaining that Arch
by stipulation of the parties) did not appear at trial because it was a
direct action defendant, and authorized execution against Arch beyond
the terms and limit of its Policy in violation of the Direct Action
Statute.... 
3. The [ trial court] permitted seizure of Arch[' s] assets above the Policy
limit, in violation of the Louisiana and U. S. Constitutions, which guard
against the deprivation of property without due process and the
impairment of contractual rights.... 
4. The [ trial court] failed to recognize that the Direct Action Statute is
procedural, and that Arch's liability can be only derivative of its
insureds' liability and instead allowed execution to proceed while the
insureds' suspensive appeal was pending.... 
5. The [trial court] improperly relied on inadmissible extrinsic evidence
in reaching its ruling while disregarding Arch' s proffered affidavit
evidence.... 
A preliminary injunction is an interlocutoryproceduraldevicedesignedto
preservethe statusquo betweenthe partiespending a trial on the merits. Stevensv. 
St. Tammany Parish Government, 2016-0197 (La. App. 1st Cir. 1/ 18/ 17), 212
So. 3d 562, 565. Generally speaking, plaintiffs seekingissuanceof a preliminary
injunction bear the burden of establishing, by a preponderance of the evidence, a
primafacieshowingthattheywill prevailon themeritsandthatirreparableinjury
2026, renderingthe appealpremature, however, Tramble did not seek to dismiss Arch's appealas
premature. Nevertheless, the appeal was not subject to dismissal, as the judgment was later signed and was
substantiallythe sameasthe orally pronouncedjudgment, andTramblewas givenfair noticeof Arch's
intentto appeal, of the grantingof theappeal, andof the perfectionof the appeal. SeeReedv. Superior
Motors, 415 So.2d 219, 220 (La. App. 2d Cir. 1982) ("The appeal, originally premature, is not subjectto
dismissal if the judgment is later signed and is substantially the same as the judgment orally pronounced, 
and the appellee is given fair notice of the appellant' s intent to appeal, of the granting of the appeal, and of
the perfection of the appeal.") 
orlosswill resultwithoutthepreliminaryinjunction. La. CodeCiv. P. art. 3601; Hill
v. Jindal, 2014-1757 (La. App. 1stCir. 6/17/15), 175 So.3d 988, 1002, writ denied, 
2015- 1394 ( La. 10/ 23/ 15), 179 So. 3d 600. 
Although a trial court' sjudgment on a preliminary injunction constitutes an
interlocutory ruling, a party aggrievedby a judgment grantingor denyinga
preliminary injunction is entitled to an appeal. La. Code Civ. P. art. 3612( B); 
Stevens, 212 So.3d at 565-66. However, appellate review of a trial court' s issuance
of a preliminaryinjunctionis limited. Theissuanceof a preliminaryinjunction
addressesitself to the sound discretion of the trial court and will not be disturbed on
review unless a clear abuse of discretion is shown. Hill, 175 So.3d at 1002. 
DISCUSSION

argues that Arch' s devolutive appeal from the denial of the motion for preliminary
injunction is moot becausethe underlyingjudgment has beensatisfiedin full. 
Accordingto Tramble, onMay 8, 2026, Arch paidtheremainderof thejudgment, 
which resulted in full satisfaction of the judgment, and Tramble filed a satisfaction
of judgment into the trial court record and moved the trial court to dismiss all
